There were a few times when I didn't even want to continue reading Crossed. I thought to myself, this is it, Meda has gotten herself into a mess she can't get herself out of, it'll end badly, just stop reading..... Needless to say, I was hooked. What a stellar conclusion to the Soul Eaters trilogy. It's rare to find a series that has all of the characters stay true to themselves while still having them discover more about who they are. 
 This is one of my favourite series (was there ever any doubt?) Meda Melange is one of the most lively, ruthless, badass characters I have ever had the pleasure to read about. Highly recommend.

Not awesome, not terrible. I admit while reading it I had to keep making myself read it, and went between it and several other books before finally deciding to just finish it and I did so quickly because I have to finish any book I start (its a weird thing I always do, even if I hate it). That isn't to say I hated it but I knew it wasn't going to be a favorite of mine. It is one of Stephen Kings less talked about novels and it feels like he wrote it with that in mind almost. 
 The protagonists are old.... really old, which is sort of.. meh, because you don't care too terribly much about their well-being when you have the feeling that they will die in a few years any how. 
 It did pull me into the story but it got sort of... ridiculous and absolutely nuts. And not in the good way. In the way where you think the only way the author can tie it all together is by coming up with something so nuts and crazy. I'd say this book isn't as plot drive as it is ... umm what's the term I'm looking for... well.. Basically it uses the crazy nature of characters and the plot to use for its message and theme. It's about abortion and I think the message here was, people who are all balls to the wall for a certain cause (ie abortion) will do literally anything for their cause no matter how nuts or crazy or ridiculous. This book is a practical satire of those said people and the lengths they will go to in order to fight a battle without end that has no winners or losers. 
 I personally liked that part, since people who argue about abortion are really arguing over something that is already legal. They can't change it, they won't change it, they're just people who are obsessed with arguing over a dead topic. They do crazy things to gain recognition by the people on their side; to basically become heroes. Oh look what Ed did, chucking dolls full of blood at the abortion clinic and got arrested! He sure does care for our cause, we need more people like him on our side! When in reality all it does is show how strongly he feels about it, while being completely unproductive. I know I just rambled but I'm stating what I believe King was trying to say in this novel. The book ends sort of tragically, but it is a bittersweet tragedy. 
 Part of the thing I mentioned earlier about  having old characters in the novel, and I mean like REAL old. That part makes you care less about the well-being of the characters, when Ralph dies you really aren't heartbroken because of his age, and also because he is exchanging his life for someone else's life.  That part sort of annoyed me, and is likely why there aren't geriatric characters in books such as these. 
 It's wort a read, but is quite long, and if you aren't really drawn in by the premise or uber curious about it, I don't know if you could sit in for the entire novel.

Everwild begins where Everlost left off. Allie and Micky McGill are wandering Everlost, working as finders. Nick has been dubbed the Chocolate Ogre and is traveling through Everlost by train in an attempt to find Afterlights and give them the coin that will take them to the great beyond. Mary Hightower is floating across Everlost in the gigantic Hindenburg, spreading rumors about Allie the Outcast and the Chocolate Ogre, terrifying bands of Afterlights into believing that she has all the answers pertaining to Everlost and that she will keep them safe. A war is brewing between two sides... 
 Everwild has the same ghostly atmosphere as Everlost and isn't missing anything that the first had. There is still adventure, mystery, and the deep sense of longing that accompanies the characters (especially Allie). Skinjacking is explored in more depth, and a twist about 3/4 of the way will make you gasp - or at least it made me gasp. Mary becomes even more of a villain, and other characters that round out the Everlost world are introduced. Shusterman has a way of making you believe that this world really exists just beyond your realm of consciousness. Even the utterly illogical always seems to have a logical explanation because it is Everlost and that is the way things are.

A Discovery of Witches has been on my radar since shortly after it came out. I'd seen glowing reviews and heard great things from friends, so I figured I should give it a shot. I received this book for Christmas last year, and finally got a chance to pick it up about a week ago. Honestly, I'm not really sure what I think. 
 Here are the basics: 
 Our main character, Diana Bishop, is a historian and non-practicing witch descended from the famous Bridget Bishop (of Salem Witch Trials fame). Not wanting to be accused of getting ahead by using her magic, Diana refuses to use it for anything aside from necessities. When the book begins, Diana is at Oxford, researching alchemy for her next project. She puts in a request for the well-known Ashmole 782, and given her credentials, it's readily provided to her. Suddenly, it seems that every supernatural creature in all of Europe has flocked to the library to watch what happens, because little did Diana know, but Ashmole 782 has been something of a mystery for hundreds of years. This super-special, super-enchanted manuscript has baffled even the most powerful witches, but Diana opens it by simply laying her hands on it. She knows there's something special about it, but given the fact that she's denying her magical heritage, she just gets what she needs and sends it back to the stacks. That's when all hell breaks loose and she requires the assistance of a very old, very mysterious, very handsome vampire to keep her safe. 
 I'm not going to lie. I really struggled through the first half of this book. At one point, I made it about five pages before falling asleep. In the middle of the day. (That is not something I do, ever.) The first half of the book is dedicated to ridiculous, painstaking, overly-detailed descriptions of what Diana is reading, what Matthew is drinking, and what everything smells like. It's like Harkness hadn't quite found her plot yet, but wanted to keep filling pages while she thought about it. The pacing does improve about halfway in, but not enough to compensate for the first half. With the improved pacing comes a fairly predictable plot: 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Can Matthew save her? (Of course he can.) 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Matthew can't save her this time, but can she save herself? (Obviously, there's two more books.) 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Can she figure out how to use her magic in order to save herself? 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 I took issue with a few things in the book that made it really hard to like the main characters: 
 * Matthew thinks it's perfectly fine to break into Diana's rooms himself -- before he even knows her. But he flies into a rage when he finds out that someone else did the same. 
 * Matthew convinces Diana to flee to France with him because of the supposed danger she's in at Oxford. But once they're there, he abandons her (probably because he loves her so much, or something) and she literally cries enough to fill a room with water. 
 * What am I even supposed to think about this marriage nonsense? Diana and Matthew kiss in front of Matthew's vampire mother, then declare their love for each other. (This is after they've known each other for approximately two weeks.) "Just so you know, we're married now," Matthew says. "Oh, okay," says Diana, as she begins referring to his children as her own. WHAT? THAT'S NOT HOW MARRIAGE HAPPENS, GUYS.  
 This book is basically just Twilight for adults, and I really wish someone would have told me that before I started, because this is not what I signed up for. 
 A Discovery of Witches is much too long, and much too detailed. A decent editor could have cut out at least 100 pages of unnecessary descriptions and backstories. A good editor could have probably taken this book down to half its length. 
 I'm not sure whether I'll pick up the next two books in the series. Harkness seems to think that by having Matthew repeatedly say, "You don't need to know about this right now, I'll tell you later," I'll be compelled to keep reading. Honestly, I don't think it's worth the effort. I was frustrated with the slow-moving plot and pages upon pages of unnecessary description. I wasn't impressed by A Discovery of Witches, but it's also not the worst book I've ever read. 
 I'll give it a generous two and a half stars for drawing me in at the very end.

 "Because now the baby was tangible. Not just a concept or a belief. Real. Excitement mixed with fear, and the desire to protect crashed through him like a burning hot wave. He staggered to his knees under the weight." 
 Unfortunately I have to say I was disappointed with the final book in one of my most loved series. It did not live up to the exciting, magical, assassin, butt-kicking book I've loved in the past. 
 To start the review, a look at Valek an Yelena. Their voices and mannerisms in the book have changed, but that didn't bother me much at all. Valek the Assassin is slowly turning into Papa-Valek, and Yelena has when she calls "baby-brain". Where Valek was more trusting of Yelena to handle herself, he seems to worry more for her safety and doesn't approve of her putting herself in danger, and vice-versa with Yelena. Out little couple is growing up and worrying about their future as a family. 
 What really threw this book off was the entire plot line. It seemed to be bouncing around everywhere. In other book in the series, groups would split and every other chapter or so would update on one group or the other. In Dawn Study, however, there were so many separate groups by the time one rolled around the reader would have forgotten what that group was up to in the first place! 
 There were also more than a believable number of kidnappings/captures in this book, even for a romantic fantasy! Every other chapter one of the characters was in need of rescue, which is disappointing for this series because I loved how the characters were mostly self reliant or always had each other to get out of the tough situations. 
 I did love that Fisk and his Helper's Guild had a major roll in this book. His little guild of street kids has almost grown into an army of their own, and they the ins and outs almost as well as any trained man of Valek's. It's great is see what started as a insignificant character in one book grow to become so important over the series. 
 Overall, Dawn Study was good. It defiantly wasn't what I was hoping for in the last book of the series, but it was good. Now I'm just left with my fingers cross for a Janco/Ari/Onora spinoff.

Beautifully written. I adored the way PLAIN KATE sounded like someone was telling me a story throughout the entire book... as opposed to the beginning starting out fairy tale-y, only to lose steam and transform into a typical 3rd person novel. That made my reading experience all the more exciting. I mean, when you read a book, you expect to either read it in first person or third person POV. And when you read it in third, you expect to hear about multiple characters (usually, at least) while also hearing/seeing how they feel throughout the story, right? 
 Well, you don't get that in as much detail in PLAIN KATE. Or at least, I don't think you do. I could be wrong, and my excuse is literally feeling as if I was teleported back into that time. I felt like I was in a dream the multiple times I opened my book up, and I think it's because of the writing style. 
 Plain Kate's life is tragic and full of heartbreak. Yet, despite that, she continues on with her life. It was inspiring. I felt bad for her. I loved her cat companion, Taggle, while detesting Linay. I felt accepted when Kate felt accepted. My chest ached whenever she struggled to fit in or felt achingly alone in the world. I was shocked when she was in the cage and the lantern scene occurred. I felt miserable for Kate. It wasn't her fault that all those horrible things happened, and yet, she's the scapegoat. It made me want to strangle Linay. 
 Interestingly enough, I felt oddly detached from this book at one point. Go figure the lantern scene would change my mind and rekindle my adoration of this dark, beautiful story. 
 PLAIN KATE is a refreshingly new addition to the YA genre. This book would be so much fun to listen to on audio as opposed to reading. (I don't do audio books, but I would definitely consider trying them out if PLAIN KATE was my first experience). Especially if the speaker had a calm, soothing voice. It would definitely be something I'd like to listen to as I settled down for the night... for the first half, at least. 
 If you're curious about PLAIN KATE, I would suggest reading if you're in dire need of a unique YA book that doesn't focus on an unrealistic teenage love (or love triangle). Like I've said, this novel is a breath of fresh air and was beautifully written. Definitely looking forward to future works by Erin Bow, and I think you should be, too (which means... go read this book, already!).

 I'm a sobbing mess. This book is the most beautiful, precious thing that I've read this year. 
 Ove is a newly retired, grumpy man who doesn't seem to know of the existence of the word "fun". But is there more to this strict old man than the appearance might suggest? When a foreign family moves next door his orderly and secluded life is turned upside down in unexpected ways, but will Ove be able to adapt and let someone new into his life? 
 I cannot begin to explain how much I enjoyed this book. It's funny, engaging and beautifully bittersweet, and Ove's character is absolutely fascinating. 
 As the story progresses we find out more about his past and I watmed up to him more and more with every reveal. 
 The 40 year long feud with his neighbour Rune, his reluctant care of a stray cat that he calls "Cat Annoyance" and his interactions with the neighbours made me both laugh out loud and at times tear up. 
 The young Swedish/Iranian family who moved into the neighbourhood was easily my favorite, especially the determined Parvaneh and her 2 young daughters. 
 I cannot recommend this book enough, and whoever liked the movie Up is bound to love this as well. Ove, Parvaneh, Jimmy, Cat Annoyance and Sonja will stay with me for a long time and I'm so glad that I got to know them. 
 I only have a minor, tiny complaint about the book... Ove is 59 years old, and I feel like the author should have made him at least 10 years older. First of all, it's hard to believe that he'd be retired at an age when most Swedes still work regularly, and also... my dad is just 2 years younger than Ove and it's hard to reconcile an image of a working, active and tech savvy 57 year old with Ove who doesn't even know what an iPad is. 
 All I'm saying is that I'd find it more believable if Ove was just slightly older. 
 Also, his neighbours are rougly the same age as Ove and they suffer from Alzheimer and Parkinson's and they are about to be taken into a nursing home??  I have a feeling that the author doesn't differentiate between an average 50-something year old and a 70-year-old, but the difference in real life is huge. 
 The age complaint aside, this is easily one of the most poignant and memorable reads of the year, so do yourself a favor and pick it up as soon as possible!

This imaginative novel has a host of characters, but there are three main characters: Aomame is a sports/physical therapy trainer, and Tengo, a writer/mathematician. The third key character is Fuka-Eri, a 17-year-old girl who grew up in a religious cult, and escaped at the age of 10. Fuka-Eri wrote an imaginative novel, and Tengo is persuaded by his editor to be a ghost-writer, to rework the novel so that it is more literary. 
 When I first started reading this novel, I was just sucked into the story. For some reason--it pulled me in. Each chapter alternates between the points of view of the main characters. After reading the first two chapters, I thought that the book was a collection of short stories. There was simply no connection between them. It takes quite a while before the connection becomes clear. And there are surprises--I thought I understood Aomame by the end of the first chapter--boy, was I wrong! 
 Although I have classified this book as "fantasy"--it really is not fantasy. It is not moralistic and would be better classified as "supernatural". The characters slip from the real world of 1984 into a parallel world of 1Q84. In this world, there are little people who walk out of the mouths of dead animals and people, and two moons. Otherwise, the story is based on reality with occasional inexplicable happenings. 
 This is also a romance; Aomame and Tengo last saw each other 20 years ago while in grade school. They both would like to see each other again, but Aomame admits that she is not willing to go out of her way to find Tengo. She prefers to leave such a meeting to fate. 
 All that said, I found the book starting to become tedious after a while. It is far too long--it could easily be cut in half without missing crucial components. The flavor became repetitive, and at a certain point the surprises petered out, and the plot became somewhat predictable. 
 However, this book was translated from Japanese to English by Jay Rubin and Philip Gabriel--and the translation is masterful. The novel reads as if it were originally written in English. Kudos to the translators!

Inspired by the new Ken Burns/Lynn Novick series, I picked up Fredrik Logevall's magisterial Embers Of War, which I'd started reading a few years ago. When I reached the chapter about Graham Greene, I took a break to read this novel. I'm not a fan of Greene's fiction, so saying that The Quiet American is my favorite isn't saying much. Greene's narrator, a supercilious correspondent who invites you to despise him on every page, is a strong character - in fact the only complex character in the book. When he thinks to himself, in the final pages,I was suddenly very tired. I wanted him to go away quickly and die. Then I could start life again - at the point before he came in.I believed him. There are a few scenes, both savage and luminous, I doubt I'll ever forget. 
 I waited until I'd read the book before I turned back to Robert Stone's introduction, which surprised me by its caustic assessment of Greene.His rendering of all the American characters as pathetic straightmen, helpless before irony, blinking in the pure light of the British characters' ordinary, instinctive decency and wholesome common sense has a darkly familiar tone. It suggests the delight of the long ago, storybook public school bully at recognizing an elaborately vulnerable mark.Perhaps that's true - but it's also true that Greene's verdict on American interventionists, however jaundiced, was prophetic, a decade before most Americans had even heard of Vietnam.

 So, apparently I have been on a contemporary kick..idk just have! One contemporary after the other. And the good news? They have all been absolutely fantastic!! But this one isn't a cute love story. Yes, there is Julian but there is far more important things going on than just Julian. I have only read one other book that deals with bullying and that was Thirteen Reasons Why by Jay Asher. That book was amazing and really impacted me. The whole snow ball affect...wow. But I'm not hear to talk about that book today..I already did my review on that one ;) 
 I don't think we as teenagers...or even grown adults know the impact we have. How one word, one gesture, one look can hurt far worse than we can imagine. We all know bullying is a problem. Millions of dollars have gone into programs for anti-bullying. But honestly, are those programs going to be what stops bullying? No. And if we are honest, we will never be able to stop it...we can try and strive...but the choice is in the people. Those people are the bullies...sometimes those bullies don't even know they are the bullies...another problem. And we can't fully understand it all at times because we don't know. Plain and simple. Those who aren't bullied can't even begin to understand. And that goes for those who aren't the bullies. 
 This book, though, gives us a small insight into the lives of those being bullied. What it might feel like, the thoughts that go on, the lives those victims live. And it hurt. It really hurt emotionally to read about what Noelle had to go through. But through it all she was strong. And I think that is where we can help. To give the people who are bullied by giving them hope. To give reassurance just with a simple smile, a simple "have a good day", or an invitation to go to the movies or what not. But like in this book...it is easier said than done. 
 Keep Holding On is a hard hitting emotional read with real life characters and real life instances. This book will impact you in more ways than one. I thoroughly enjoyed this book. Susane Colasanti's writing was believable and likeable. Some books just tend to leave little impacts on your life...and this was one of them. Honestly, sometimes there were parts I felt like it was missing something but not enough times to where I was willing to put the book down..for good. Do I recommend this book? Yes. :) And as far as rating goes....

***5 'Hello Emotional Rollercoaster' Stars*** 
 I knew going into this book that I'd be in for a hell of a ride. There was no way it couldn't be based on all that I'd come to know about Julia and Austin in the first Wright books, but holy hell did this one do a number on me and there were times when I seriously wanted to toss my Kindle in the freezer (it's a tad bit kinder than tossing it against the wall), but at the same time I couldn't stop reading it. I needed to know what these two would put each other through and see if they made it out alive, but more so I needed to see if they could overcome all of their baggage because the spark between them burned so bright that it's was so obvious they were each other's forever. 
 Admission time: I didn't like Julia and Austin half the time. I didn't. They both frustrated the hell out of me more often than not and made me want to put the book down, but then they'd have a moment that would grab hold of me ~ whether it be together or separately ~ and I was sucked back down the rabbit hole. They both are damaged and simply pretending to be okay. Julia does a much better job than Austin, but she has her demons. But what kept me reading, and rooting for them, was that underneath their issues were two people with bruised, yet golden hearts that needed to a safe place to land so they can heal and shed the burdens that plague them. 
 Their road to their HEA was all kinds of rocky, not only because of the whole enemies to lovers thing, but all of the other baggage they were both carrying, and let me tell you they both have a shitton of baggage. But what had me rooting for them to not only get together, but get their shit together, were the sparks that always flared when they were simply close to each other. They had a connection that, even when they couldn't explain it, jumped off the page and needed to not only be grounded a bit but nurtured so could evolve into something wonderful. Thankfully, it did but not without a lot of work and some very unexpected 'come to Jesus" moments and in the end I loved where they were at when all was said and done. 
 The Wright Mistake was a full on roller coaster ride, but one I'm more than happy to have been on. Ms. Linde touches on some very sensitive subjects, but I feel that she did it with a lot of respect and wanting to give as much of a true to life depiction of them and not gloss over the dark parts. As I am a sucker for ensemble casts/well written secondary characters and keeping up with the ones we've already met, this book had it all for me and I loved hanging out with all of them There were a few unexpected twists in this one, and there is one that I am sure will cause an uproar with some fans of the Wright family, but I'm pretty sure that the ultimate end result will be amazing to see.

In this modern coming-of-age novel, we learn about Charlie and his experiences through the letters he is writing to an anonymous friend. I usually do not like this style of writing, but it worked for me in this novel. One of the first events that Charlie reports is the suicide of his friend Michael. Next we learn a little bit about his immediate family and his Aunt Helen. Aunt Helen is deceased but she has played a crucial role in Charlie's life. Even though Charlie has experienced a tragedy and lost important relationships, his life improves when he meets Sam and Patrick. They are seniors and sort of adopt Charlie like a pet of theirs. Sam is a girl and Charlie immediately forms a crush on her. Patrick, her stepbrother is gay. He becomes a close friend to Charlie. Throughout the novel Charlie experiences a lot of intense experiences-drugs, sex, and the Rocky Horror Picture Show. 
 The Pitfalls of Being A Wallflower 
 Charlie is quiet and introspective. His English teacher remark that "...sometimes people use thought to not participate in life." Charlie is a passive person-he just sort of lets things happen to him without exerting much free agency. Like the time when he allows a couple to invade the room he is in to have sex-in front of him-without objecting. When he later realizes that the sex was really a date rape, instead of reporting it to the police or confronting the guy during the crime, he slashes his tires to get back at him. In another instance he allows Patrick to kiss him because Patrick's heartbroken even though he isn't gay. 
 Charlie 
 The events in the novel along with Charlie's feelings and actions throughout seem unbelievable. For instance, he cries a lot in front of his peers. He also asks for advice about sex from Sam, specifically how to tell his girlfriend he isn't ready. His friends Sam and Patrick don't seem to mind his idiosyncrasies, but most of the other kids at school think he is a freak. I thought he was strange too, but once I found out what is haunting him I came to understand why he is the way he is. 
 Quotes Teens Like  
 "...sometimes people use thought to not participate in life." 
 "Charlie, we accept the love we think we deserve." 
 "And in that moment, I swear we were infinite." 
 !!!!Spoiler Alert!!!! 
 Charlie is a victim of sexual abuse by his aunt. He has repressed the memory but a sexual experience triggers it. I congratulate the author for addressing this topic. While our society no longer denies that sexual abuse occurs we still often picture the perp as a stranger when it is most often a relative or close family friend. All victims feel ashamed, but the sexual abuse experienced by a male child and perpetrated by a female is the most shameful secret of all. Kudos to Chbosky for treating this topic with Perks.
Loved it.

It was before she became the hardcore addict that we see her in the series, but you can see the beginnings of it here. Chess is assigned to work with the Black Guard on a case in order to help her decide what section of the Church she wants to work in after she graduates. She's very vulnerable from the places that she grew up, and she very much wants to stay with the Church, is frightened when she thinks that anything could jepordize her future with the Church. We see the same insecurities that follow her throughout the series and it's still sad, yet Chess has always been a fighter and she wants to survive. This is a nice addition to the story, giving fans more information on Chess's early background with the Church.

I loved this book! I've been a J.R. Ward fan for years and I always worry that for some reason I won't like the newest book as much as I liked the others (my taste changes, I don't connect with the story, etc). Luckily I loved this story just as much. 
 This story includes many points of view as is the way in the Black Dagger Brotherhood series, with a focus on Trez and Selena of course. I was delighted, and kind of surprised, to get Rhage's point of view and Paradise's point of view, giving a nice lead into Blood Kiss. iAm and his lady love, which I didn't realize he'd get in this book, also experienced their own love story.  We also catch up with Xcor, Layla, and more. I'll admit that normally there is a story line that I get more excited about than the others in the book (besides the main couple) and I want to flip through the book and just follow that line and come back to the rest of the book after I've been satisfied. Though I don't do this, that's not how it was meant to be read after all, I usually have to suppress the urge to do so. Not in this book. I loved all of the story lines equally this time around. I wanted to know what was going on with everyone and how it'd pan out so much that I didn't feel the urge to do that skip. I'd get there. 
 I will admit that the ending isn't traditional for romance, but don't let that stop you from reading.  While it's not a traditional, the couple is together and mated, the ending made sense and it was a strong love story, made stronger by the fact that Selena's time was limited. I don't know if there would have been enough conflict and emotion to keep their love story as engaging without that ax hanging over their heads. And J.R. Ward doesn't leave us hanging. While there is grief, there is also an amazing show of everyone coming together. It was uplifting to get a reminder that they're more than just a band of warriors. They're a family and they take care of each other. They really do. On Trez's part there is also acceptance and a form of happiness. While I don't wish death upon any of the characters I was happy and satisfied with this ending. It was handled well and left me waiting impatiently for the next book. I couldn't ask for more than that  
 Overall, this was another great book added to the series. If you love the Black Dagger Brotherhood then this is a must buy and a must read. If you're new to the series, go pick up Dark Lover and catch up. It's a series full fighting, loving, and great world building. Just like Earth, the world of the Black Dagger Brotherhood is forever changing and along with an amazing love story you will get a world that feels real and engaging.

I could not wait to read Hero when I first heard that Samantha Young was writing this standalone story, and I was not disappointed at all! This book was everything that I have loved from Samantha Young in the past, and was also so much more. It was captivating and interesting, and I absolutely couldn't put it down. This book sucked me in right from the start, and ended with me staying up way past my bed time because I had to finish. 
 After finding out some awful things about her father, Alexa Holland has worked hard to turn her life into one that she can be proud of. She works hard and is determined to be nothing like her father. When she meets Caine Carraway, she knows that she needs to apologize for the horrible things that her father did to his family. But Caine wants nothing to do with her, and doesn't care that she is trying to find some redemption. But when Alexa gets fired from her job due to Caine, he offers her a job working for him. Caine decides to make things as hard as possible for Alexa in the hopes that he will push her too far and she will walk away for good. But Alexa isn't going anywhere easily and is determined to show Caine that she is nothing like her father. The more time they spend together, the more the tension between them increases until it finally explodes. Alexa wants Caine and is convinced that they can find happiness together, but Caine knows that he is not the white knight that Alexa wants him to be. 
 I really liked Caine. He was sexy and confident, to the point of being cocky and arrogant at times. He had his moments where he was a jerk and tended to say some horrible things, but I found myself loving him anyways. He had so much pain from his past, that it was clear to see he had never really dealt with anything. As soon as he would say something awful, he seemed to genuinely feel bad about it which made me think that he wasn't as horrible as he tried to come off as. He and Alexa brought out so many emotions and feelings from one another, that things were very intense between them. It was clear to see that the passion between them would explode one way or another, and sometimes they ended up hurting one another when they didn't mean to. Alexa had just as many issues as Caine did, and I think that she really understood him. She was strong and relentless, and I loved that she never gave up on Caine. She was so dedicated to showing him what they could have, and I really liked that about her. No matter how many times he hurt her or pushed her away, she saw it for what it really was. Though sometimes a character like hers can come off as weak or a doormat, Alexa didn't to me. She wasn't weak, but rather stronger than anyone knew. She was exactly what Caine needed and I loved seeing her help him grow and heal. These two had so much chemistry between them, and they were super hot together. But I really enjoyed seeing them get to know one another and form an emotional bond as well. 
 Overall, this book was so good and I really cannot recommend it enough. I loved the characters and how complex they were. Caine had so much beneath his surface and it was clear that we didn't know everything through most of the story. He had battled through so many hard times, and I knew that when his past was finally revealed that he felt awful about how he had become the man he was. He did what he had to do to survive and make something of himself, and I really felt for him because he wasn't proud of how he had achieved that. But I was glad that Alexa was able to show him that none of that mattered to her and that she loved him for the man he was and not what had been his past. If you are a fan of Samantha Young's you will really enjoy this book, and if you are new to her this is a great place to start. I really loved Caine and Alexa's story, and I cannot wait to read more from Samantha Young in the future.

I generally don't like knowing about authors, musicians, and artists because they can only complicate the art itself. Orson Scott Card's anti-civil rights agenda made me want to dislike this book or find the seeds of his bigotry within the pages. And perhaps with a more thoughtful read it is there, but that was not my experience reading Ender's Game. It is a good, perhaps great book. Even knowing the plot beats ahead of time (I had previously read the graphic adaptation) I found this book to have great inertia. The manipulations and training provide interesting pseudo-psychology and military tactics. The biology of the enemy is very creatively explored and the treatment of time and space is carefully handled and makes this book borderline "hard sci-fi". Of course is does use Ursula K. LeGuin's "ansible" (a device for faster-than-light communication), but that has practically become sci-fi cannon at this point. I was particularly pleased how well he balanced their genius and the fact that these are children. The characters are the foundation of this story, which is rare in sci-fi and what makes this a classic.

I have every sympathy with anyone facing a 'celebration' they do not wish to celebrate, and who climbs out of the (ground floor) bedroom window to escape from it. Like Water for Elephants, the protagonist is an elderly man in an old people's home where he does not wish to be. His spirit is unbowed, even if his legs aren't as steady as they used to be. Unlike Water for Elephants, Allan Karlsson is not going to run away to a circus - instead he simply wants to go as far away as possible on a 50-krone note. Thus starts a bizarre sequence of events that, once you skip back through his life (which you do, in suitably digestible chunks), becomes totally in keeping with his extraordinary twists of fortune. 
 Since Allan is 100 years old, the chunks tracing his life start right back in the 1900s. It's a life lesson for any teens agonising over their careers after their exams - you can have a successful and interesting career so long as you take the opportunities that come your way. Admittedly, the opportunities that Allan takes are somewhat crazier than most of us would face, but then we were not born in Sweden with a father who had the misfortune to fall out with the Bolsheviks just as the Communists took power in Russia. It's enough to make anyone avoid politics forever, which is exactly what Allan does. Nevertheless he gets embroiled in one dangerous political situation after another - well, there was a lot going on between 1920 and 1990 in Europe and America... and Russia, Siberia, Korea, China, Japan and Iran, too. Allan manages to get into all the political and revolutionary hotspots. 
 In between the flashbacks we are treated to the police pursuit all over South Sweden after he does his disappearing act, and the crazy events that he's mixed up in. 
 The writing is dryly humorous, full of fun, yet absurd at the same time, with wonderfully rounded and somewhat inept characters. It's rather like a Swedish Hitchhiker's Guide to the 20th Century - it shoulod have Don't Panic written helpfully on the back. 
 I absolutely loved it - with a slight sadness that I thought it dropped off at the end. But I still give it five stars - since I'd have given it six if I could. 
 It's a bizarre, somewhat Nordic noir romp that I thoroughly recommend to adults who like something clean and off the wall with a smattering of wacky history thrown in. 
 Best Read of 2014 Award

This was an intense book that handle some heavy duty issues and how people attempt to cope with some hard choices they have to make in their life. Noah Hutchins and Echo Emerson are two teenagers who I believe are kindred spirits. They both have to deal with some hard core situations in their lives, that most teens never have to encounter in their lifetime. 
 Noah is dealing with his family as he knows it, ending in an extremely tragic way. Him and his brothers are without their blood parents, and thrown into the foster care system and separated due to circumstances that have occured. This is heart breaking for Noah as he has a deep love and bond with his younger brothers, and he just wants to be a family again. He is also terrified that they will suffer in this system that has already failed Noah in an awful way. He wants to fight to win custody of his brothers after graduation, and take them away from the people who have them now; Noah does not feel he can trust any adults at this point in his life. 
 Then we have Echo, who is covered in scars on her hands and arms. There was some kind of accident that involved her and her bipolar mother; the problem is that Echo has no recollection of what happened the day that changed her "normal" world forever. Echo lives her life alone in a crowd of people, and insecure as most of her school friends have talked behind her back and stated that she was crazy. She is ashamed of her scars, and wears gloves to hide them away from the world. 
 Both Noah and Echo are seeing a therapist (very reluctantly!) whose name is Mrs. Collins. She is an eager therapist; but Noah and Echo really don't feel like trusting her or talking to her. When they meet one day in the waiting room, they don't like each other on sight. As time continues they are thrown together in a tutoring situation where they decided that they can help one another out. They desperately need each of their files, so they develop a plan to sneak a peak at them. Echo needs to remember what went on the night with her mom, and Noah needs the address of where his brothers are so he can accumulate evidence against their foster parents. 
 Echo and Noah grow very close, develop an unbreakable bond, and fall in love. There story is one that is heart breaking, heart warming, and at times entertaining. I love these two as a couple. It is also nice to see both of them grow up through the story. Noah starts off with such a chip on his shoulder, tattoes, and just plain angry with the world. Echo softens him and teaches him so much about life and himself. Echo begins basically in hiding...from her scars to not being involved with her friends at school; Noah teaches her that she is beautiful inside and out and that her scars are something that she shouldn't be ashamed of. I love the personal growth that they both have, and I love how they have found each other. 
 This is a story that musn't be missed, there is so much depth to it and it gets you thinking. I personally love a good book that will have you sitting in your chair and thinking about how you can relate to the characters. I close with a quote from Noah when he was talking to Echo: 
 "Why is it when people are proud of me that my life sucks?" 
 "Because growing up means making tough choices,and doing the right thing doesn't necessarily mean doing the thing that feels good."

Dude, omg this book is freaking awesome! Rich lent it to me after I saw it on his shelf and gleed a little over it. I love love LOVE the cover and had been attracted to it a while ago, but then I wasn't so sure once I'd read the blurb. Zombies? Really not my thing. So it was just one of those "eh, maybe one day" books... until this weekend. 
 AND IT WAS SO AWESOME! It's set in an alternate 1880s Seattle, where part of the city has been walled off for the past fifteen years to attempt to hold in the Blight - a poisonous yellow gas in the air which turns people into "Rotters", aka zombies. Zeke and his mother Briar live on the Outskirts, the safe part of the city, but one day Zeke decides to venture into the walled off part - because you see, it was his dad who created the "Boneshaker" which ravaged the city and unearthed the blight gas. So then Briar naturally freaks out and runs in after him... 
 Ooh it was so adventurous and wonderful and totally gripping, and just the right amounts of terrifying. I decided Rotters/zombies do fall under paranormal wtfckery but this wasn't one of those annoying supernatural books at ALL. The Rotters were terrifying and evil and there to be destroyed before they could destroy you! I loved it so much more than I was expecting to and was hooked right from the start. I haven't read so much steampunk either but this definitely makes me want to read much more. The alternate Seattle was a fascinating place and I love how there was that feeling of modernness mixed in with 1880s historicalness. 
 Definitely want to read the next in the series now, oh boy! Itching to get hold of a copy is more like it. :D Also, as well as the cover, omg the sepia text on off-white paper was so darn pretty! :D

The battle is over, but the war is just beginning for Logan Gyre. Both he and Kylar are bound by vows they wish they hadn't sworn, but honorable enough to attempt to keep them. Conflict explodes between the friends and between countries. Logan's desire to live by his principles clashes with Kylar's desire to see him take the throne. As each man strives to do right, a war looms that will shape or reshape the entire world. 
 As before, it's hard to write any kind of summary without spoiling major surprises. The action starts strong and never lets up. Picking up directly where the second book left off, this one delves straight into the aftermath of the battle. The characters shine once again: Kylar and Logan alone would make the book worthwhile, with their complex friendship and the theme of light and dark played out between them. But the story doesn't stop with Kylar and Logan. Vi struggles with the consequences of what she did at the end of the second book. Dorian chases after his visions; Elene chases her heart and the voice of the God. Past and present and future intertwine, illuminating old events and giving shape to new. 
 There were only a few minor flaws. One chapter summarizes an event that happened only two chapters ago, as though originally this had not been a scene and was only later added but someone forgot to remove the summary. Uly is practically dropped as a character, which, given her potential and her role in the second book, was a little disappointing. The Seraph also appears only to disappear. 
 Overall this is a wonderful conclusion to a fresh, powerful trilogy. It's a shame to leave this world, but with any luck Brent Weeks will eventually publish more so I can continue to laugh and cry and worry over the people who have grown so familiar. Many of the themes from the first two books reach their fulfillment here, so read the trilogy in order. I rate this book Highly Recommended.

Aw. Why does this series have to end? I want to keep reading more. If you enjoyed White Cat and Red Glove I think you will also enjoy Black Heart. It is a very satisfying ending to this series. 
 Holly Black created a seemingly realistic world that is actually paranormal. The writing is just so good and effortless you don't even realize that it's not all true. The events happen at a good pace and the suspense really keeps you on your toes trying to guess what will happen next. 
 I love Cassel. He is extremely street smart, charming, and has a bit of snarkiness that comes out when he is nervous. I love that he is a flawed character - he knows it, and while he doesn't like that about himself, he has come to accept it and makes no apologies for it. Cassel has grown as a character since the first book. He is so much more comfortable with his ability. He tries so hard to stay on the right side of the law, but things always seem to catch up with him. It's hard not to want him to always choose to do the right thing. 
 I think this was a great ending to a fantastic series. Although I do feel that there is enough storyline and plenty of characters left to explore to continue the series.

At the beginning, Doctorow gives a pretty good explanation for writing this book. The surveillance systems that the government use have become pretty crazy in recent years. We don't even know half of the stuff that they have on us, because we don't realise that they can track our movements via credit card, phone location, and travel cards. They can even recognise (with reasonable doubt) a person by gait analysis. Yet we have very little power over changing this, and with each new technological development, there's probably a way to exploit it to harvest more information about us. 
 With this in mind, Doctorow is after creating a very plausible world where, following a terrorist attack in San Francisco, the government increase surveillance and privacy invasion to a point that even puts teenagers under the microscope, tracking their whereabouts, and putting their every game and social event under suspicion. 
 One kid, Marcus, after being held illegally and interrogated, decides to rebel against the ever-increasing 'Big Brother' style world he's been plunged into. While not the most believable character ( a little bit of Mary-Sue begins to emerge as the story goes on), he provides the reader with a lot of clever ways (if you have a handle on programming) to protect your information, ranging from extra password protection, to encryption of data. There really is a lot of great stuff explored here, when the gang of 'rebels' are trying to communicate in secret, and to even just browse the internet without getting spied on. 
 The plot is good: it keeps hopping from one event to the next, each one getting more dangerous and risky for the young gang. The feeling that the government are always one step away from removing your basic rights really shine through as the biggest threat in this story. 
 Do read this if you aren't fully aware of how capable the modern world is of knowing anything they want to know about you; and if you think that it's just playing to paranoid fears within us, jsut remember this was written well before the Snowden leaks, and the discovery that our every email can be read by a paranoid agency who also believe its within their legal jurisdiction to have backdoors built into all phones to be able to mine private data if they fell the situation warrants it.

I thought that these were brand new stories but I had already read 2 of them in previous anthologies. The Summer People is an absolutely perfect modern fairy tale that I originally read in Steampunk! An Anthology of Fantastically Rich and Strange Stories. Secret Identity was the best story that I read in Geektastic: Stories from the Nerd Herd. 
 All of these stories were fantastic. This is a book that I'll have to reread because there were so many layers to each story. My absolute favorite was The New Boyfriend which, like the majority of this collection, was a new and strange take on your average ghost story. Kelly Link packs more story in a few pages than most writers do with an entire novel. Her characters are always interesting and each story left me wanting more. 
 The Summer People- A modern fairy tale full of farey folk in the Appalachian Mountains in North Carolina. 
 I Can See Right Through You- This was a sort of ghost story. Imagine a 40 year old Kristen Stewert and Robert Pattinson at a nudist camp making a sort of Ghost Hunters tv show. 
 Secret Identity- A REAL superhero convention. 
 Valley of the Girls- In the future rich kids stay out of the public eye, their parents hire other children to pretend to be their kids' public Face. Also, forget Kabala and Scientology, all the cool kids are into Egyptology. Pryamids replace penthouses. 
 Origin Story- This seems to take place in the same reality of Secret Identity where the world is full of real superheroes. As an added bonus this story takes place in a real life location that I have always been interested in. Land of Oz Theme Park This might be the creepiest coolest place on earth, Follow the Yellow Brick Road to the Abandoned Land of Oz 
 The Lesson- A gay couple go to a wedding on a secluded island but it's hard to have fun when your sickly surrogate is about to give birth a few months early. This story was ambiguous but also had some strong imagery including a parade of wedding guests in cheap bridal gowns traipsing through the jungle to a wishing well and black bugs spewing out of a work of taxidermy. 
 The New Boyfriend- My favorite. A teenage love story mixed with ghosts and robots. What's not to love? Heartbreak, jealously, and female friend dynamics with a science fiction twist and a huge creepy factor. 
 Two Houses- Ghost stories told by astronauts who then find themselves in a ghost story... 
 Light- A stew of the bizarre. Pocket universes, shadows coming to life, and people in an eternal sleep all set in Florida.

Madline Sheehan never fails to shock and amaze me with her mad writing skills. Never have I been so captivated, awed, and even slightly sick to my stomach all at the same time! 
 Unattainable offers a double feature for the price of one. First we have the infamous Cage (son of Deuce) and Tegan (daughter of Dorothy). (I wonder if I will need a family tree when this series is all said and done). 
 "Take it, Teacup....Be my girl." 
 Tegan and Cage grew up together in the club. She has always loved him as a best friend and more. When she was in her teens, she gave her virginity to him. Cage (aka man whore) broke her heart because he didn't reciprocate the love she wanted so badly to give him. Things went from bad to worse when her mom was shot (go back and read book 2 to rehash that drama). Tegan fled Montana and went to San Francisco where she is making a way for herself. (She also has made a way with shacking it up with ZZ (remember Danny's ex).) Every time Tegan comes home, Cage tries to make nice with his old friend "Tea cup". She will have nothing to do with it. Finally, her sassy mouth drives him to pull full on crazy and he just takes her. It is hot and violent to say the least. This is probably the least tender of all of the couples in this series. Cage will do anything to keep Tegan. He wants to claim her as his. There is a great deal of Drama (with a capitol D). I found both of them to be very immature. I felt the love they had for each other. I was happy that they were able to work things out in the end. 
 The other love story in this book was beautiful and heartbreaking. Ellie is home to take care of her dying mother. She is attacked in a dark alley when Dirty saves her. Dirty is broken. The abuse that he had to endure as a child was heart breaking. (Be warned....this content was very unsettling!) Watching these two connect in an intimate way was slow and beautiful. You were rooting for these two to find peace in each other. Their story was a sweet addition to this book AND it complimented the Tegan and Cage drama nicely. 
 "Michael," he heard her say, her voice soft. "Please look at me and let me show you what love is." 
 Overall, I enjoyed this read. Eva and Deuce are still my favorite (even though Deuce made me pretty mad in this book). The action is fast paced, the drama continues to build, and the follow up with the other characters only offers more interest in future installments. Who doesn't want a HEA for these biker bad boys and girls?

Bryn is just barely dealing with being the human alpha of a werewolf pack when she is given another challenge. Shay, enemy brother to Bryn's friend Devon, has called the Senate together to discuss murders he believes are being done by a female Rabid. While a male Rabid would simply be killed, a female is too valuable. Bryn knows the female in question is Maddy, who Bryn released from her pack after Bryn was forced to kill Maddy's boyfriend Lucas. Now Bryn must find Maddy and convince her to return to the protection of Bryn's pack before the other packs find her and claim her. 
 I'd read Trial by Fire a while ago, so it took me some time to figure out all the details of what happened in the final showdown with Lucas. There was no info dump / summary here; I just wished I had read the last book more recently. 
 As always, I enjoy the political nature of Bryn's position and how she must deal with the werewolves, humans, packs, and loyalties around her. The appearance of ghosts (or shadows) and the connection to twins was a really interesting part of the story. Bryn's relationship with Chase was sweet... I'll leave it at that, because the ending drops a lot of changes that make me eager for the next installment!

Rating: 5 
 The Low Down: What if you grew up knowing that your kiss would one day cause the death of your true love? This was no idle threat from an overbearing father, mind you, for Blue Sargent has no father. When you come from a family of clairvoyants and psychics, you tend to believe them when they make predictions such as this. Blue doesn't see ghosts and can't read Tarot cards, but her gift is valuable. Her talent is in amplifying the abilities of those around her.Every year on St.Mark's eve, Blue and her mother, Maura, go to the churchyard that is on the old corpse road to see who will die that year. This year, though, is the year two things changed: Neeve, Maura's half-sister goes instead of Maura; but, more disturbingly, Blue sees a ghost. She speaks with him, learns his name (Gansey), and determines that he attends the local rich-boy boarding school, Aglionby Academy. Blue has made it her policy to stay away from boys in general, but especially those there. They are known as the Raven Boys because of the school crest they wear.Gansey is a student at Aglionby, and though his family is indeed filthy rich, his reason for attending the esteemed Academy has less to do with education and rubbing elbows with his wealthy peers than finding the ley line and where it leads. Out in a church parking lot the same St. Mark's eve, Gansey sees and hears nothing. However, his tape recorder tells a different story. He hears his voice answering questions...and a girl's voice asking them.Soon their paths cross, and Blue also meets Gansey's friends Adam (the scholarship local), Ronan (the angry one) and Noah (the quiet one). When they join forces, it leads them to a mystery, a killer, loss, brutality, burial and rebirth. 
 Best Thang 'Bout It: The writing just pulls you in, gently. After the shortest of whiles, you don't even realize you are reading. It's like hiding in a tree where you know there's life beyond its canopy, but you are cocooned inside and no one can see you or disturb your world. I love fantasy where it really might, really could be possible; the lines here are not really that far-fetched or invented. My words cannot do the author's words justice. 
 The interconnecting stories come together very nicely. I don't try to solve mysteries ahead of time (I like for them to unfold), but sometimes things are so obvious as to be obnoxious. Like, "Hello! Here's a clue! Over here!" This story was not that way, though if you are one who likes to figure things out ahead of time, it probably wouldn't be super difficult here. 
 I'm Cranky Because: I'm not really cranky about it, per se, but I can't tell you what I was, let's say, confused about, because it would be a major spoiler. 
 Should You?: If this is a genre that you like to read, and especially if you enjoyed the author's writing in her wolf series that started with Shiver, you will love this book (beware that it is not the same type of book as Shiver, though). Emphatic yes. I cannot express any better how lovely the writing is in The Raven Boys. 
 The Raven Boys by Maggie Stiefvater was published on September 18, 2012 by Scholastic Press. 
 Genre: Young Adult Fiction Fantasy Paranormal Romance Mystery 
 Ages: 14 and up 
 You Might Want to Know: Profanity and underage drinking. 
 Find this book at Amazon and Abe Books.

This book was such a heart drowning, heart shattering and heart warming adventure that I could not put it down. I have to say that David Estes works will never cease to amaze me. Fire Country was a novel built upon treachery and tears - it digs deep into your soul. That's the best way that I can word it. I swear, the author has this magical ability to make you feel everything that Siena does. She was the absolute optimal MC a reader could ask for - I was so attached to her (more so than any of the previous Dweller MC's and that means a lot) maybe it's because Siena started out as weak that I grew this imaginary bond to her but as the plot thickens Siena begins to shake off her hatchling shell. 
 Another aspect that I truly believed was the most heart warming was that of Circ and Siena - if there were ever two people made for each other it would be these two. Such a golden couple - When I thought Circ died I thought I was going to be physically sick. I didn't understand how David could do that to me, us, everyone who grew to love Siena's second half. To be honest I grew frustrated with the book at that point - was emotionally broken because those two were nothing without each other. But alas, all turned out good in the end.  
 The plot was brilliant, Siena's father was a monster and was in fact a vile, disgusting man who only saw women as essentially livestock. The mystery of the Wilde was also a key factor that was interesting - and who can forget Perry? My god, I laughed a lot at this one (especially later in The Earth Dwellers!) It was a great addition - as weird as it may sound. The introduction of the other characters was also quite enjoyable - however, my favorite were the Siena and Circ portions. 
 Overall, Fire Country was a beautifully written novel that I adored with every fiber of my being. In the end, we see the "weak, skinny, runt" of a girl become stronger and evolve from a child into a woman who knows how to stand up for the rights of her people, The Heaters. Once again, some of the most genuine story telling I've ever had the pleasure to experience and recommend it to all.

Still, I could easily remember what it was like to feel alone and lost at that age, and I did feel emotionally connected as a reader. Overall, it was a book that I had a hard time putting down because (like Clay) I wanted to know how all of these puzzle pieces fit together. I liked the use of cassette tapes, I liked the ending, and I liked the overall structure of the novel. I think what hurt my reading experience was Clay. Early on we know that he has feelings for Hannah but doesn't know her very well. Not knowing her POV yet, it was easy for me to feel like he fell into the 500 Days of Summer trope where he saw her as someone who she wasn't and was in love with the idea of her, not who she actually was. My opinion changed a bit when we learn that she did feel something for him too, but it definitely influenced my reading experience for the first half of the novel.  I'd recommend this to any reader who is interested, especially since its one of the best in this subgenre and has sparked so many other great books.

 In Winter of the Wolf, Cherise Sinclair's second in a series about a community of shape shifters in the mountains of the northwest, the reader is treated to a fun, light read about a fantasy world in which were lions, were bears and werewolves live a precarious existence among humans. 
 After a chaotic upbringing in various foster homes, Breanne Gallagher hates change. But change comes in a big way when her sister is killed and she is attacked by a monster that changes from man to beast and back again. She travels to Cold Creek, based on the only photo she has of her birth parents. Her landlords, Zeb and Shay, turn out to be werewolves, who serve as guardians of the other shape shifters against hellhounds-demon shape shifters that prey on humans and shifters, but prefer shifters. But hellhounds are only vulnerable in a couple of places and fighting them requires getting so close that injuries are almost inevitable. 
 Zeb and Shay are intrigued by their lovely little renter, and amazed by that fact as shifters aren't usually attracted to humans. It turns out, of course, that Breanne isn't human, but a shifter who has never made the shift. And the three of them have to face hellhounds-both in Cold Creek and in Breanne's home, which leads to major issues with the community. 
 While I'm not usually a fan of fantasy, good writing can overcome a lot and Cherise Sinclair is nothing if not a good writer! Breanne is strong, caring and brave, and her heroes are the same. There is some very light BDSM in the book, along with a menage relationship, and lots of hot, steamy sex. I had no problems enjoying the world of Cold Creek and the story of Breanne and her men.

I absolutely adored this book! What a wonderful, enthralling debut that captures teen angst and the weight and confusion of romantic inclinations and identity. 
 Amanzimtoti: The Ridge follows Wayne du Preez, as he starts his last year of high school with his best friend Travis and his girlfriend Jess, and is confronted by the sudden and unexpected reappearance of his childhood best friend, which leaves him with him exploring an unhealthy inner turmoil of feelings. 
 Once I got a few chapters into this book, I found it incredibly hard to put down. I was completely sucked in by Wayne's internal conflict vs. Kyle's persistence of a relationship of any form vs. Jessica's unwavering dedication and kindness. I honestly loved every single character and the relationships and dynamic built between all of them. 
 I loved that this book used South African slang. This, coupled with the luscious descriptions of the landscape, made me truly picture the surroundings and the lives that these teens led. I also really appreciated that there was a glossary of these terms at the back of the book, so even if you had no knowledge of South African slang, you could still understand what these characters were saying, and be further immersed in the authenticity that Carmen-Shea Hepburn was trying to create. The use of this slang also added to the character of these teenagers, and helped greatly in truly believing that there were actually teenagers, and added to the honesty and realism of all of them. 
 One of the most important parts of the books was of course the budding, and oftentimes fraught, relationship between Wayne & Kyle. I loved the slow burn of the relationship, and the longing and meaningful glances between them, however I equally couldn't wait for them to get together. It is a hard task to create a love triangle and have readers care about both relationships involved (in this case, Wayne-Jessica and Wayne-Kyle) however I believe Carmen-Shea Hepburn has mostly achieved this (I'm still rooting more for Wayne & Kyle but Jessica is so incredibly sweet that I want the best for her too). It is also a testament to how good of a writer Hepburn is, that she was able to make me understand both Wayne's and Kyle's viewpoints. Both of them have experienced homophobia due to the nature of their relationship, but still this doesn't want to fully stop them. 
 Yes, Wayne blames Kyle for the kisses. 
 Yes, that definitely isn't nice of him. 
 But yes, I can completely understand it. This is a boy who is incredibly scared of allowing himself to have feelings for Kyle. It could jeopardise everything for him, and from the glimpses we've seen of his family, they'd make his life absolutely miserable if they thought anything was going on. He's trying to protect himself and those around him, but that doesn't mean he doesn't want Kyle. The struggle that Wayne has between his heart and his head is nice to see, and it's going to be interesting to see this further explored in the second book. Again, the fact I feel for Wayne, who's just trying to protect people, and for Kyle, who knows what he wants (and knows that Wayne wants it too) and is unwilling to settle for anything else, is an indicator of how excellently Hepburn has built this universe with these characters in this setting. 
 Kyle, to me, never seemed like a bad guy, even though it was obvious that he was actively pursuing Wayne. I did feel bad for Jessica, but I also felt as though the relationship between Wayne and Kyle was unstoppable. Even though we did see Wayne blame Kyle for the kisses, and act like he was just reacting to anything Kyle did, and though he was almost an unwilling participant, he did invite these things. Again, Wayne wants Kyle but is just afraid of what it could mean, and it is wonderful to see this intense struggle of wants explored. 
 I do love that Wayne is essentially what people may class as a jock, but he's also incredibly sensitive, finds it hard to make friends, and has deep secrets - he's absolutely not a two-dimensional character. 
 In fact, none of the characters in this book are two-dimensional, especially Travis and his conflict between loyalty to his sister and loyalty to his best friend, and how he struggles to handle this later on in the book. Even the side characters that we see, such as members of the rugby team, and the popular girls, are all shown to be different to the main characters. Even though this book very much centers on four people, there is a definite change in dialogue and personality of every single character, even when there is minimal dialogue for side characters compared to Wayne, Jessica, Travis, and Kyle. 
 Personally, probably the only downside of this book is that for me, too much time was dedicated to Wayne's internalised homophobia and self-harm and anxiety issues. I understand that this is incredibly important, and I loved that it was in the book, but I believe we saw one too many instances of it, and as a reader it made me slightly uncomfortable. I did not count the number of instances this happened in the book, however it starts in one of the first few chapters, when Wayne sees Kyle again for the first time in eight years, and near the very end of the book too, and is a major theme throughout. Intentional self-harm (plus a case of accidental self-harm) happens a lot, and is the most important coping mechanism in this book for Wayne. When you consider that this book is full of angst, you can imagine that he will turn to this a lot, however I do still think that the amount of times we did this happen was a little too much, and some of the cases could have gone unspoken but implied. This would have still achieved the exact same message, but again, it is incredibly important to see these issues discussed and described, especially in the case of teenage boys. 
 Another minor point that I didn't really enjoy was when Kyle insinuated that Wayne was only in a relationship with Jess because he wanted to be with Travis. That kind of threw me as I had never seen that kind of relationship between Wayne and Travis, and it seemed a left-field comment for Kyle to make, and then for Wayne to seriously consider.  I'm glad that Wayne came to the conclusion that Kyle was wrong, but it still seemed like a weird almost sub-plot to me. 
 The ending frustrated me beyond belief, but only because I wanted to know what happened next. The abrupt ending offered me no satisfaction, but knowing that there is a second book coming, that is going to hopefully further explore the relationship between Wayne and Kyle, is comforting.

It irked me that she asks to leave for their trip early and then goes and makes sure he knows that she doesn't care about the trip. I also couldn't understand her obsession with Nate Holden (though I can't question her choice in guys). 
 Abbey grows tremendously over the course of the novel. I am glad that I didn't stop reading because of her attitude because I grew to love her spunk, especially after she finally begins to open up to her dad (and stops being sarcastic all the time). 
 Funny story about the romance. I was wondering why Abbey obsesses over Nate Holden, and then I saw this really great guy and asked why she couldn't like him when... voila! She opens her eyes to the right guy. And they are so cute together! I am sorry for the first guy she kisses. He isn't a bad guy, and I wish there could be a happy ending for him. Who knows? The ending is left open for musing, and I'm going to believe that there is hope for a guy like him. 
 I didn't guess who the pretty boy of cloud and skies was until Abbey asked him who he was. He is a really special boy and, in a roundabout manner, gives Abbey the strength to heal and grow to appreciate her second chance at life. I love how the story played out. On a Dark Wing is an amazing story about death, life, and healing. Jordan Dane is a brilliant writer who took me on an emotional ride where I empathized with the characters, cheered for them, and cried my heart out for them.

"Wait," said Valentine. "Listen. You ask: 'what makes man so great?' he quoted. "Is it that he re-created nature? That he harnessed forces of almost-cosmic proportions? That in a brief time he has conquered the planet and opened a window onto the universe? No! It is that despite all this, he has survived, and intends to continue doing so." 
 I came to Roadside Picnic like so many others, via Tarkovsky's Stalker, but Tarkovsky uses the novel as a vehicle for his own melancholic reverie. The novel has a different tone. It has its philosophical moments, but the stalker Red Schuhart is not a philosopher by any stretch. He's a smuggler and black marketeer, and the Strugatskys use his profession to spark the story into action. 
 The backdrop of the story -- a visit by extraterrestrial beings who leave behind technologically advanced "trash," which turns out to be very valuable contraband -- is pure science fiction, but the story line revolves around a simple smuggler trying to beat the system and support his family. The system is corrupt and the "visit" is slowly poisoning the planet, but there's nothing fantastical about that. Maybe that's why Soviet officials had such trouble with a book that is on its face non-political. (Boris Strugatsky outlines these troubles in an afterword in the 2012 Chicago Review edition. ) It's a many-sided novel -- a sci-fi adventure story, an economic and political commentary, and in a less obvious way, a philosophical rumination on human happiness (or lack thereof.)

 The Evader (Logan) lives a dangerous life as he races through the bustling manhattan streets. He cannot be beat. He has only one friend that assists him on his mission. What he wants is put in jeopardy when he meets Kaci. He is drawn to her. 
 "She stood out like a sparkling jewel amidst the cesspool of thugs , gangsters, and bikers who arrived in groups. She came alone, watching the finish line from the seat of her flashy pasta rocket."

This is my first exposure to Emily St. John Mandel's writing, and I very much enjoyed her technique. I was hooked into the plot pretty quickly and then struggled to put it down. 
 The book is based upon an epidemic that forces civilization into unknown territory. It's not simply a survival saga or a linear progression of the outbreak, how it happened, and the results. Instead, this story is told from multiple different timelines and various perspectives. This is perhaps my favorite aspect of the story. The story unfolded in a way that made sense to me despite how it frequently jumped from time and place. For me, this enhanced the tale. It allowed me to develop my own conclusions or ideas before the event was completely revealed to the reader. It made me feel more attached to the story. 
 Some larger, overarching themes that I've taken away from the book: 
 -An actor dies on stage and a man tries to save him. The impact of Arthur's life on all of those he was close to at some point then followed by his last moments of self-reflection realizing the numerous mistakes and errors he made. I was sad for him because I knew that when he realized this was minutes before he would die. Jeevan is acting on his instinct and training to save Arthur. He wasn't always a hero, in fact, in his past he took advantage of them. His progression shows us that we can overcome our past and define ourselves how we want.  
 -An epidemic of catastrophic proportions breaks out (the telling of this part of the book reminded me so much of The Stand & Captain Tripps). This defined everyone, one way or another. This delves into our basic instincts and human nature. 
 -A traveling group of actors and musicians journey town to town performing in the post-apocalyptic world. Their tag line sums this up perfectly "Because survival is insufficient." I enjoyed pondering what this would mean in this world and what a person would need emotionally once physical survival is no longer in a state of flux. 
 -An encounter with a prophet and his religious followers.Someone who monopolized the catastrophe for his own personal gain. Who preyed on the persuadable and weak. I was impressed by how his character was brought to life. Seeing his progression to the prophet was some of my favorite parts to read. What really got to me was how believable this scenario of events was. It seemed like such an easy, logical progression when the full story was revealed, which is chilling.  
 My only reason for a 4-star rating instead of 5-star stems purely from the ending. I was disappointed at the commonness of it and felt slightly let down. In my opinion the facing the prophet after the kidnapping and disappearance was anticlimactic. Although I was happy to see one young person in the doomsday cult recognize him (the prophet) for what he was . I still recommend this book and intend to read more of her work.

Audibook this time, which is probably the most disappointing thing about my experience with the book. I really would have wanted to go back through a couple passages and read in all the words, making up the images in my mind and sitting in vivid Africa for a while. Instead I was driving through uncomfortably muggy England with some moments of not complete focus. 
 Despite that, it's still great. It approaches a lot of new ground that I've not read about before and it does it in a way that makes it easy for the reader to approach. It won't teach you about a full and authentic experience of African life, but it gives you enough to work with and informs you of the important things. I know more about Patrice Lamumba than I ever thought I would, I know more about African food and language than I ever thought I would, and I am absolutely certain that driver ants are fucking horrifying and oh, jesus christ, I never want to be near them. 
 But there's a story under all that and it's a great one. The central characters are strong and well defined, the prose flicks between stark and truthful to flowery and picturesque, and even though there's no major antagonist or particular set piece the plot has this feeling that it's always moving forward, the characters are always trying their best to survive, and something is always happening. 
 Oh, and something that I've really got to mention is the approach to point of view and character voice. There's five perspectives that we hear from in this book, all from the first person, and I don't think I've read anything that even comes close to defining the characters so well simply by their prose. You could give me five different sentences from this book with no context and I like to think I'd have a good chance of identifying who said it. I'd get in the car after work or in the morning and turn the book back on and, nine times out of ten, even with no mention of characters or unique circumstances, I would know who was talking. It's impressive enough that it makes me a bit mad to think about it. 
 Probably the only bit that I wasn't fully sold on was the epilogue/final chapters. Following up with everyone post Africa/post Kilanga works, but feels like maybe a little overlong and ends up dispelling a lot of the tension and personality when it hops from years to years.  That being said, that dip was maybe a single 7/10 section in a 10/10 book, so it's hardly a reason not to read it.
