 "Unfortunately, the term 'bad' took on a whole new dimension a little later when I found myself sititng at the kitchen table, examining the food in my bowl." 
 Now that I've had a few experiences with books found in the 'New Adult' genre, I have found that the outcome can either be really good or really bad. That is the possibility to happen with any book, but it's always a 50/50 chance with these guys. As I predicted, this was one of the ones in between, but more closer to the "bad" side. 
 This book started off as nothing special. I did have some thoughts to not finish it, but as I went on, it got a little better, and then worsened. The plot was the main problem because it was predictable, and it basically wasn't even there. 
 Mystery? I don't see it. This book is supposed to be classified as a mystery novel, but I didn't strongly see it. Sure, there was some bits and pieces of suspense, but nothing unbelievable. Every book is almost the same. 
 So this is about some snobby bitch named Sasha, who is filthy rich. And so is her father. She's nineteen, by the way, and acts like she's in her thirties. She clubs, goes to parties, whatever you can think of that's scandalous. Then her father makes sure that she has a bodyguard with her at all times, and well, he's a snob as well. At first, they can't stand each other, but as their "relationship grows," they fall in love. 
 That's all what this book really was, and some tiny bits of action when Alex fights some guys, including Sasha's ex because he won't let anyone touch his "client." And then, Alex is so "mysterious" but dreamy at the same time, and she's going to try and find out who he really is. 
 So I did have some problems with this book. Some major, some minor. In the beginning, it sucked. The middle was okay, and the ending sucked as well. Something really made me want to stay, and I guess it was Sasha's bitchiness, because I felt "in the mood" for that type of behaviour. On a rainy day, I'd just smack the heck out of that girl and walk away. Thankfully, the weather was nice and sunny, hot. 
 I guess if you're looking for a no-plot nothing special story, then this is for you. It's not 100% worthy to read, but it has its positives. 
 So.. the characters basically made up for the downer parts of the book. Sasha was a total bitch, but at the same time, I loved her. She had her moments when she was smart, snarky and totally witty. I loved her as a protagonist and reading her POV was much better than being bored. She kept me up and going, and made up for the bad parts... a little at least. 
 Alex was okay. I just pictured him as a macho idiot, but he was funny. I was in the mood for a funny read, so he and Sasha both kept me going. I felt like he verbally abused her a lot (haha) but together, they made a real cute couple. Automatic ship. 
 By the end, I was upset with this book because I wanted it to be better. But in the inside, I knew that it wouldn't please me too much. Overall, this was just an easy, fun read, if you're looking for something like that. Recommended, sure, but not for everyone.

 Relentless had a lot of buildup to the big reveal for the super horrible thing Claire did that will make everyone everywhere hate her forever. Unfortunately because there was so much build up, so much talk of how horrible the thing she did was, that once it was revealed I was disappointed. Just like really that is it? That is why everyone you ever tell will hate you forever? Never mind that lots of women do the same thing every day. Well maybe they tell the guy first, but still lots of women make the same decisions. It was just...I know she has issues. I know her mom and then foster homes messed her up. I know she needs to see someone to deal with her issues because she just doesn't deal with them herself, but I was still disappointed. 
 At the start of the book Claire has issues. Lots of them. She checks out sometimes and that is not good. I mean what if she is walking across the street and she just checks out as she doesn't seem to be aware of her surrounding when she is out of it? She meditates all the time to try and get rid of all of the bad memories. This is how she lives her life. She is also super suspicious of all guys thanks to her mom. Well Adam takes two seconds to fix that! She is pretty much instantly attracted to him and starts to not really care. It felt like she had major issues, but they were suddenly fixed when she met him. Sure she still freaked out sometimes, but after a while she was just fine. No more checking out when he was a round! Great. Perfect. It is that easy! No more problems. 
 Adam seemed okay. He was kind of...something about him felt off to me. He seemed to like Claire a lot, but there was something about him and the way he was with her that didn't sit quite right with me. Not that he was bad for her or anything. I really don't know what it was about him that I didn't like that much. Plus he professed his love right away which was not really believable. Then he has secrets as well, secrets that I would say are worse than Claire's, and he shares with her. They really weren't that bad, but I can see why he would hold himself responsible. By the end of the book I thought he was okay, but at the beginning something didn't sit right with me. 
 So you go along in the book and Claire doesn't share her past with Adam. Doesn't share that her ex is the rock star Chris. Doesn't share why she dropped out of college (because of the oh so horrible terrible thing she did that everyone will hate her for!!). Doesn't really share much with him. Then of course it comes out at the worst possible time because of some girl who shared it because I am not sure why. She was jealous of Claire having dated Chris? She liked Chris? Something. Either way it happened and I thought oh that is all? Of course then Chris is upset with Claire and they talk and he tells her how he wants her back and he will stop at nothing to get her back. That whole thing, how Chris acted, seemed very threatening. Dangerous almost. Like he might actually hurt Claire and he doesn't really care what Claire wants. If he really loves her shouldn't he at least consider her feelings? Oh well, I really did not like Chris or the way he bullies Claire. Then Adam is too forgiving of everything and I just didn't really like either of them. By the end of the book I felt like Adam was too good for Claire and Chris would be a nightmare for her. Really I think she should spend time to get better for real, go to therapy or something, and then once she is healed add boys to the mix.

I was very eager to read this book when I downloaded it from Project Gutenberg - I did after reading and immensely enjoying The Moonstone by the same author. I couldn't wait to read something else by Collins. Instead, I ended up waiting for some months, and decided to read it now on the occasion of a group read. 
 Well, never was a disappointment so terrible! In the beginning (let's say the first half of this very long book) I thought I might have to give up. It was so boring I couldn't go on reading. It's definitely easy to see that it was originally published in instalments - the author clearly needed to drag on and on. 
 Moreover, while I had found The Moonstone to be a very modern book, so much so that it didn't read like a 19th century novel, I think this one is very rooted in its century. What with the way in which women are seen (they just want to stay at home and cook for their husband - *rolls eyes*) and so on. True, Marian is a very strong character, but she herself says she's only a woman, as weak as those of her sex are. Might be this was consciously provocative on the author's part, as in, he puts such words/ideas on Marian's lips, while at the same time portraying her as a strong woman. Might be, but I didn't like this all the same. I'm not saying I was expecting a feminist point of view from a 19th century male author, but I'm exhausted by this diminutive opinion of women. I just can't stand it anymore. Full stop. (So maybe I shouldn't read classics, probably). 
 However, in the long run I was rewarded, as the story grows more interesting in the second half of the book. The mystery is ever more present, and the gothic feel, too. That's why I ended up giving three stars to the novel as a whole. Moreover, the writing was extremely good. But this novel is not going to stick in my mind forever. Far from it, I'm afraid.

Okay. I'm finally going to write this review. I needed time to process :P This review will be littered with spoiler sections, so seriously, don't click on them if you haven't read it yet! 
 *deep breath* 
 I wanted to love this book so much more than I actually did! Don't get me wrong, there were some really great passages and I still think Stiefvater does a really good job of developing all her characters equally, but. But. The ending was not satisfying to me at all. It's not so much that Glendower was really dead the whole time. That kind of made sense to me. We felt the same disappointment that the Raven crew did. That was fine. What I hated was that Gansey lived. I know I sound like a hypocrite because I've been saying for weeks that I wasn't ready for Gansey to die, but somehow, by the time the book was finally released, I was. It feels like a cop out to have Gansey come back to life, and I don't feel like the world supported it, either. It's not like in Harry Potter where we all knew Harry was a horcrux, and that was how he wasn't actually dead. I don't know. I think it would have felt more poignant if Gansey had really passed on, and we had to see the gang deal with the grief and repercussions of that. From reading other reviews on here, I know I'm not the only one who wanted Gansey to stay dead. Or not even that I wanted him to, but that it felt like Stiefvater was cheating at her own game to keep him alive.  
 Another big letdown for me, besides the ending was the extremely lackluster conclusion of Noah's storyline.  He deserved more :'(. But I will say the creepiness factor he had in this book was on point, and man, when Blue made that comment about how she had kissed a DECAYING GHOST HOLY SHIT  I was so taken aback, because, yeah! It was also very sad though, cuz it was such a tender moment when it happened. Stiefvater is generally pretty good about writing these moments that just punch you in the jaw with emotion, so I don't know what happened with the ending... anyway. 
 But speaking of scenes that should have been really emotionally intense but just... were not... Blue and Gansey's kiss was such an anticlimax. I felt nothing! I definitely haven't cared as much about their relationship as Adam and Ronan's, but I was still excited for them to have their moment. Frankly that whole scene was weird. Ronan's basically dying in the background, and Gansey and Adam are fistbumping goodbye? Sure...  
 The treasure hunters/Lamounier/Seondeok/etc. just were not fleshed out enough for me to care about. I have grown to like the Grey Man, but even he got short shrift in TRK. 
 Let's not even talk about the demon . Plot device much? Overall I feel like the plot suffered in this final book, and while I'm glad she prioritized character development with the gang because I care about them so much, I was still frustrated by how stilted the plot felt. 
 One character that also felt like a huge plot device was Henry Cheng.  It's not that I didn't care for him, I do. He was funny and had some great lines, but he did still feel like he was shoe-horned in to get Stiefvater out of some plot holes. I do, however, love that he's going on the Grand Tour, so to speak, with Bluesey. OT3! ;)  
 I kind of loved the reveal about Artemus, Blue's father. It did explain a lot about Blue, and it felt true to the series' world. 
 Okay, now let's talk about Pynch. Y'all know I have been shipping this hard since book 2. I was SO appreciative of Adam's comment about Blue's body still being attractive to him , funnily enough, because bi!Adam is so important to me. I was really glad to see Stiefvater take that route with his character, and not go the GFY route, or worse, the "bisexuals are gay/lesbian in transition" stereotype. So thanks for that, Maggie, seriously. It's so refreshing to read characters like me that aren't stereotypes but are still complex. Anyway, the kiss between Ronan and Adam  felt, to me, a little rushed, and didn't have the emotional payoff I would have liked. But I was still glad to  finally see Pynch made canon, beyond subtext or teasing.  It might seem like such a little thing to straight folks, but LGBTQ representation, and authentic representation at that, is so important in YA. I wish this book had been around when I was a teen. It would have given me ~life~. 
 I hate that we didn't get to see Maura/Calla/the rest of 300 Fox Way at the end.  I wanted closure! Alas. 
 It kind of hurts me to give this finale less than five stars, since I definitely consider the first three books in the series to be five star books for sure. But I have to give this one a solid 3.5. There was just too much left unresolved, and a lot that didn't feel true to the series as a whole. Maybe upon a re-read I'll change my mind, but this is where I leave it for now. 
 Editing to add: I really did love Blue in this book. I always appreciated her of course, because duh, openly feminist character is kind of my favorite. But she really shone in this one. Especially the moments with her and her parents. I empathize with her a lot.

This is not an easy book to read, partly because of its subject matter. It's set in WW2, in occupied France, and mostly in Saint Malo. The book follows the stories of a blind French girl, Marie-Laure, and a bright German boy, Werner, who is a genius with radio equipment. 
 I enjoyed the double entendre in the title: referring to the electromagnetic spectrum, of which radio waves are a part, which plays such a big role in the story, and the visible light spectrum, that tiny portion which we can see; and the hidden light of humanity, the individual stories that were murdered and obscured by the war. 
 The writing is really beautiful. There are a number of passages that I reread several times even though I read this book very slowly to savor it. 
 The only negative comment I have is that due to the construction of the book, it is difficult to follow events. It jumps back and forth from one character to another and back and forward in time. 
 Nevertheless this is a great book. It will be interesting to see if it stands the test of time. 
 Here is one if my very favorite lines from the book. "Every hour someone for whom the war was memory falls out of the world." This echoes a thought I have often had and I'm very glad that books are still being written and movies are still being made about this most momentous event of the 20th century; when humanity showed itself at its very worst and at its very best. We owe it to those who lived through it to not forget the horror and the triumph.

 Illuminae is not your regular type of book. It is basically a case file full of documents and recordings from the spaceships. Yes, the whole story is told through files and reports. I know it sounds crazy. I know some people might be skeptical about this. Trust me. It works. Some people might complain that there is no character development and character depth due to the lack of description. Personally, I was not bothered. I saw the character development even without description and long narrations. The way I read this book was by listening the audiobook while following along with the physical book in front of me. By doing this, I had the sensation I was watching a Si-Fi movie unfolding in my head. The visuals in the book were awesome. It had blueprints of the spaceships, drawings, lists, imagines... It was amazing. Oh! Let's not forget about the audiobook. IT HAD AN ENTIRE CAST!!! Different voices for different characters. Sound effects. All you want! It was...I do not have words to describe it. That awesome it was. So, I highly recommend listening the audiobook while reading the actual physical book. Each, character becomes unique and it is much easier to remember who is who and what he/she/it does. The story is action packed. When you think you solved one problem a million, more problems appear out of the blue. At some point, the book gets some freaky horror vibes. You know, Walking Dead (TV show) horror type of vibes. It is just sooo rich in the feels. Oh-Oh! Let's not forget about the Terminator (movie) vibes too! 
 Is it wrong to say that my favorite character was AIDAN, the artificial intelligence software gone rogue? For a computer program, AIDAN was the most complex character in this whole story. I am so glad AIDAN appears in the next book too.  
 This is a survival story in space. How cool and tariffing is that! You do not need more information! Just go read it!

 When the h encounters him as his housekeeper, he is beyond the pale. A complete and total reprobate, he will engage in blackmail, kidnapping and even murder if he feels he can justify it, and he can always justify it as he is the Duke of Montgomery. I hate the whole Heathcliff types, but E. Hoyt sold me on the hero. The abuse that warps him is detailed and convincing. She provides a solid background that explains why he is the way he is. I went with it because it was fun to see the Duke unthaw. Does he unthaw. He's still just as shallow, self-serving, but he has a heart for more than just his sister. 
 What I enjoyed most was his total arrogant acceptance of of his own superiority in the face of her repugnance of him. Actually in the face of anyone. The H is incredibly shallow at times which made me laugh although it detracts from his status as a romance interest. 
 One of my favorite moments is when after just getting back from rescuing the h from the dogs he set on her (The h had inconsiderately rescued the heiress he kidnapped and was going to marry against her will.  The H is shallow and unrepentantly vile at times, and I loved him. In real life, I would run like the wind, but as a fictional hero he is ...unusual. I remember thinking at the end, I hope they don't have children. They are a couple I would love to read more about in subsequent books.

The Juliet Spell by Douglas Rees has a beautiful cover and intriguing synopsis, so I was looking forward to reading it when it became available on NetGalley. Unfortunately, neither the plot or characters managed to retain my interest. 
 Miri wants the part of Juliet in the production being cast: she decides to cast a random spell to get some extra oomph behind her for luck. Unfortunately, the fame spell she performs doesn't do what she expected. What it does is bring William Shakespeare's younger brother Edmund into the current day. Luckily, he is charming, attractive and acting-savvy. Maybe he'll bring her a little luck after all? 
 Edmund manages to be interesting for about two paragraphs. He ends up making out and eventually sneaks out to be with shallow girl (Miri's main competition for the part of Juliet). Miri, of course, still angsts after him hard. He is shallow, silly and a wuss (which, unfortunately basically describes Miri as well). He cries all the time! Hello: not manly. Not hot. Also, Miri's mom pretty much accepts his presence right off the bat. He is from the past? No problem. He is gonna stay in my home? Sounds good! Not realistic at all. 
 So the entire book is basically made up of Edmund either crying about being in a new place or macking on shallow girl. Miri spends all her time either repeatedly obsessing over Juliet or pitifully following Edmund around. I found them both annoying; I wish there had been some real character development! 
 So, definitely not the book for me or one I'd recommend reading. If the plot sounds intriguing to you, I'd go for Saving Juliet by Suzanne Selfors instead: a girl gets sent back in time to Shakespeare's Verona. I think it's a cute read, and a lot more entertaining!

 I actually read this in two days, stealing time from the hideousness of dismantling the house (including ten thousand books) for pest control. The house is put back together, and I'm still thinking about this smashing debut novel. 
 Scarlett is sixteen, and a private eye. We find out fairly soon that she graduated from high school two years early, but she printed up cards to post around local schools for cases. We also find out that she solved a fairly hefty murder case (which for a time made me think there was a novel previous to this), thanks to some training from her cop friend Emmet, but she's never been able to solve her father's murder, and it still eats at her. 
 Equally gnawing at her is her mother's painful cancer death, that galvanized Scarlett and her sister Reem in different directions: Reem became more devotional to the family's Islamic faith, as well as determined to become a doctor; Scarlett has pulled away from her faith, turning her back on anything that she can't touch, taste, see, or hear . . . can't control. 
 But when a nine year old kid hires her to investigate her brother's suicide, Scarlett finds herself questioning everything. Including herself. 
 Though we never find out why a devout Islamic family named their kids Scarlett and Reem, we don't have to, as Scarlett positions herself as an outsider looking in as she deals with the fallout of her decisions. Meanwhile she has to rely not only on Emmet but on her handsome friend Decker, whose mother Delilah runs a local diner, where Scarlett is always welcome. Delilah and Decker are Jews; Delilah and Scarlett's mom were close, so there's an understood acceptance and respect for others' faiths that was refreshing to see in YA. 
 Scarlett is angry and tough, throwing herself into situations she knows are dangerous. She is also slow to trust, a wariness that can work against as well as for her. Consequently there is a lot of high octane violence in the novel. I think if you like the show Veronica Mars, you're a likely audience for this novel, as Scarlett's first person voice is smart, sassy, introspective at times, then all-stops-out on the action. There are some very intriguing side characters, a mystery with a fantastical edge, and satisfying twists and turns. 
 A terrific debut. I hope we get to see more of Scarlett.

Okay to preface this review, I just wanted to say that I've seen a couple of great reviews from readers in the lgbtq+ community discussing the ace rep in the novel. And it's come to my attention that the representation is extremely inaccurate and even harmful. As a result, I've decided to remove my rating but this review will still contain my original thoughts; however, I will also link a few reviews that describe the problematic rep in my review. 
 I won't lie, I recently got into manga and anime so I was automatically drawn in by the cover. However, I was very wary of possible cultural appropriation, so I looked up more information about the author/book and found out that one: she's white, two: this book was apparently patreon funded, three: her dedication was to Yamamoto and Kubo (the creators of the anime Yuri on Ice). The last one was a huge red flag because that just screeches "Weeaboo" to me. But honestly, I thought I would give it the benefit of the doubt because I'm an anime fan myself so I get it, you know? But there are so many ways to show appreciation for other cultures without crossing over to the point of appropriation. 
 Aside from Xander's love for manga, I was initially interested in this book because of an ace mc. I'm a huge champion of diverse novels, so I was so excited about this since I haven't read very many books featuring a character on the gray spectrum. That being said, I feel like I can't speak accurately about its representation so here are two reviews in particular that thoroughly discuss the problematic content: 
 https://www.goodreads.com/review/show... 
 https://bookstogetlostin.wordpress.co... 
 Since I'm talking about rep, I'll go ahead and add in my thoughts about the inclusion of Japanese culture here. I think it would've been alright if the main character was just fascinated in manga and wanted to pursue art as a result, but the fact that the college was "Japanese culture-soaked" yet no character was Japanese had me questioning so many things. And the random shrines and background history of the town were completely unnecessary. In fact, it was a bit weird and really didn't add anything to the plot except to remind the readers that "hey! It's full of Japanese culture, remember? Cool stuff!!" 
 Also, *sighs* the use of Japanese language. Again, I totally understand when you discover a new culture and become fascinated and want to learn its language. That's fantastic, learning new languages is a great thing, and I'm a huge proponent of learning about different cultures. But it's one thing to appreciate the language, and another to straight up fetishize it. There's literally zero reason for Xander and Skylar to speak Japanese, especially just randomly in a conversation (that's lowkey Weeaboo 101). Anyway, before I start ranting, I'm going to switch over to things I liked. 
 Problematic content aside, I actually liked Skylar and Xander originally and enjoyed their interactions and relationship. I thought they were really cute together. I liked the minor characters as well, especially Unc and Zelda. The overall story arc was a bit cliche but cute. I think it did contain solid themes like acceptance and self-identity. In terms of plot, I felt like the "plot twist" at the end was unnecessary. It was really added drama that didn't need to be included in the first place. The book is already 400+ pages long which is more than usual for a romance novel. The plot didn't really drag, but it did feel noticeably long (as in I felt like I had been reading it for a long time). I think a lot of parts could have been cut without dramatically affecting the plot. 
 Overall, I think that Antisocial has some bad representation which overshadows what could've/would've been a really cute contemporary romance. I think people can still read and enjoy this novel, as long as they also note the problematic content.

I finished this a couple days ago (and the next three in the series) and I'm still having a hard time putting my reaction into words. As my teen daughter would say, the feels are just too big. So I'm going to do my best on this one and hope it applies to the series as a whole as much as to this specific book and keep it relatively general (because there's no way I'll be able to do this for every book in the series and I don't plan on being so detailed in future volumes). 
 While the book is structured as a mystery, that's actually the weakest aspect of the novel. It's not that hard to piece the whodunit together and really, I find that I don't much care. About the mystery. What makes the book stand-out fantastic is the characters and relationships. And I don't just mean the main characters, though that's the best part. 
 Clare is an Episcopalian priest in a small town in the Adirondacks. She is warm, kind, active, and caring in a way that true Christians strive to be. Which would make her cloying if she weren't so honestly and perfectly human at the same time. The members of her congregation are all fully-developed, complex people of faith as well with a realistic (in my experience, anyway) mixture of kind and venal, saints and hypocrites working together (often in a single person), sometimes overcoming their basest instincts and sometimes not. This book would stand out as one of the best depictions of an honest Christian community even if it never got to the second part of what makes it so awesome. 
 Russ is the chief of police in this small town. He's a true and honest servant of his people, working to keep peace in a town fallen on hard times and with a hearty mixture of the desperate and the priveleged--a potentially explosive combination. He has integrity in spades and an honest devotion to the law and doing what's right. He's also heavily married. 
 Clare and Russ are the highlight of the book as their relationship grows from honest trust and respect (with minor, uh, and major, bumps along the way) to something... more. By the end, it is absolutely heartbreaking as Russ and Clare become aware of what the reader has suspected for some time--that they are perfectly matched, almost made for each other and that they have no way of doing anything about it without breaking both of them into something less than they are now. The poignancy of this is heartbreaking in its tragedy and purity and humanity. 
 Which makes it seem like the book would be heavy. But that's the genius of Julia Spencer-Fleming--she manages to pull off that powerful emotional impact without losing the hope that lies at the heart of faith and integrity. It is easy to forget that Christianity is, at heart, a faith for the fallen and that its promise isn't ease or success or protection from harm but rather comfort in affliction and the eventual achievement of grace. Infusing a hint of grace into the promise of heartbreak (and making both real and powerful) is an amazing achievement and I am so happy to have found it in this story.

Amanda Briars is an accomplished writer in early Victorian era England, whom is only one week shy of turning 30. She has never known the passion of being with a man, so she hires a man for one night to rid her of her virginity. On the night of her birthday, an unknown man with black wavy hair and eyes so dark of a blue they are almost violet shows up on her doorstep. Regretting her decision, and thinking this man is the 'hired' male prostitute that she requested, she tries to turn him away, but Jack wont have any of it, making light and fun of the situation with his charming ways. Without divulging his full name and true propose for being there, Jack an Amanda have a passionate interlude, but he decides then and there that he won't take her virginity. 
 Weeks later, Amanda attends a party, she stumbles upon Jack once again, finally learning of his full name and true nature - he's a rake and publisher whom plays a bit dirty. She is yet appalled but yet still allured by him. He blackmails Amanda into letting him publish one of her earlier written works, if she doesn't agree, he will tell of their passionate interlude. But he doesn't just want Amanda's novel, he wants her in a packaged deal. Not wanting word to get out about their one steamy night together, she agrees to his terms. From that point, Lisa takes you on a steamy passionate journey between Jack an Amanda that ends in a HEA. 
 I am sure this comes to no surprise that i loved this book. Lisa Kleypas can do no wrong in my eyes, all her books becomes a favorite of mine after I finish them an I treasure them for years to come. Jack was a bit of a rascal, I just loved him. He was so charming that he was deadly - with his twinkling mischievous eyes an grinning smile. I can see why Amanda fell for him, how could you not? He was just plum delicious in every way. Not only was he wickedly charming, he had a big passionate heart when it comes to people whom he truly cares about. This was just a great book from the beginning to the end, capturing your attention straight away, which I love when books do that. I hate when you have to read about 100 pages before you are like 'Hey, this is gonna be so GOOD!'. As always, well done Lisa, you will always remain as one of my favorite Historical Romance authors.

 This book is an okay book and a quick read. The story and the world is fairly original and interesting; a good premise. The characters are hit and miss. Some of the children seem kind of interesting, but many of the other characters are very flat and undeveloped. Overall, I recommend this book for anyone who enjoys typical YA fantasy novels. I wouldn't say it is anything explosively amazing, but it's an okay book to pass the time and some other people seemed to have really enjoyed it. 
 My issues with this book is that though the world, the peculiar children and the loops are all interesting and pretty original, the story isn't really. It is a very typical story. Bad guys vs good guys and where the main character thinks the world is totally normal and then finds out it's not really. Main character then decides to team up with the good guys to fight the good fight. The bad guys are quite obviously and directly bad. There is no depth to their madness. They are not misunderstood, nor have they fallen off some righteous path. They are by the book bad guys (and so, of course, they are allied with the token historical straightforward bad guys: Nazis). The good guys are not only pretty typical 'we just want to be free to live in peace' good guys and they have the added element of being innocent children. On that note though, why would they still mentally be children? If their timeline is continuous, then shouldn't their stream of consciousness be developing into adulthood even if their bodies aren't? I mean you could argue their brains are limited physically and so they still have kid brains, but by that argument their synapses (as being part of their physical selves) would also be restored at the changeover meaning all new memories would be forgotten and therefore no continuous stream of consciousness could be established. Major plot hole. 
 Aside from this, another major factor in the story is that huge disaster could have been avoided if things were just communicated earlier. This is something that is really way overdone in YA literature and is very annoying as a reader. In this book it was Miss. Peregrine saying that Jake needed to say immediately if anything out of the ordinary was happening that could be a sign of creature that eat people. The same kind of creature who killed his grandfather, whose murder was blamed on a pack of dogs. Yet, for some unfathomable reason, the group of sheep that had just recently been torn up in the exact same manner and the strange newcomer who orders raw meat doesn't seem to warrant any mention.  
 In general, this book seems like it is trying to mimic a John Green novel and throw in some fantasy. It doesn't come together so well. It is a quick read to pass the time, but it is not extraordinary. In fact, it is super ordinary. I will not continue with the books.

Antho is a surveillance desk jockey. He witnesses a bad-ass, Matrix-looking man murder Antho's jerk boss. Instead of turning the assassin in to the authorities, he decides to take the sexy, unconscious murderer home with him. 
 This story takes place in future reminiscent of Blade Runner. I really enjoy science-fiction that takes place in this kind of urban, slick, gritty setting. Genao does a good job of painting this world without giving you so many details that you begin to doubt it or overthink things. He gives you just enough specifics and leaves the rest to the imagination - which makes the world stronger, in my opinion. 
 The writing style is amazing and gorgeous. I love the way Genao talks and describes things. 
 One of the things that works in Genao's favor is that he is using one of my all-time favorite tropes: the "take the wounded, sexy, dangerous man home and nurse him back to health" trope. This is a great trope. I always love to read stories and books that have this plot. Of course, it can be garbage (see my review of LABOR DAY by Joyce Maynard for proof), but luckily Genao does it right. He even adds in a little amnesia for extra drama. 
 Lastly, I want to tackle the characters. They are not very fleshed out - but then again, consider that this is a romance AND a short story. Assassin-man is a badass killer who wears a leather duster and has lightning-fast reflexes. Antho is a lonely man who apparently has no friends or family or acquaintances and is so consumed with lust for assassin-man that he ignores repeated threats on his life, and the apparent psychosis/amnesia of his lover. 
 Anyone who knows me is familiar with the fact that I don't like people with a temper. This is softened in this story by the fact that perhaps assassin-man is lashing out physically because he is frustrated and confused because he has amnesia. I, personally, would not put up with constant death threats and extensive destruction of my personal property - but then again, this is a romance. This is a review that compares the actual play onstage in London with the script in book form (with thoughts on the general story as well). Spoilers are hidden. 
 I watched the play in London on 4 August (Part One) and 5 August (Part Two) and finished the book a few days later - so I had everything from the play fresh in mind. 
 Firstly I want to say that the play was beautifully done. All the illusions and effects used to achieve magic was ingenious, to say the least. The audience was wow'ed over and over again and we all gasped and 'oh!'ed and clapped in unison when something particularly brilliant was pulled off. This is obviously something the script lacks; as it is not a novel, there are no in-depth descriptions of how a spell works or how something magical happens. This means that your imagination is working over-time, relying on everything it has learned earlier from the books and films to fill out the gaps. My guess is that this is easier for some people than others. 
 Something else which I've seen in several reviews already; the fanfiction vibe this script has. It is true, it does. But in the theatre, this is not obvious at all. This script was made for the stage, and theatre is a very different form of entertainment from screen and books - it relies heavily on its audience and the ability to constantly keep up the pace and the wow-factor. Thus an overload of jokes and over-the-top plot points have been incorporated, making it seem a little far-fetched, at least on paper. I can tell those of you who haven't seen the play that this all works rather well onstage; it keeps the audience going and we all laughed along with the jokes (especially Scorpius') and sat on the edge of our seats when something exciting was happening. 
 In book form all this falls a little flat - again we miss out on the effects onstage that supports many of the plot points that seem far-fetched on paper. The jokes seem one too many. The characters seem like ghosts of themselves, because we lack descriptions of their tone, their facial expressions, their gestures. All that we get onstage, and though some characters didn't seem like the perfect casting, most of them did a brilliant job - especially Harry was absolutely perfect and sounded and acted exactly how I would imagine 'our' Harry as an adult would. 
 Plot discussion time: again addressing the fanfiction vibe. 
 I have one part of the plot that I cannot cope with and I will not accept it as being true: Delphi being Voldemort's daugther by Bellatrix. With a character like Voldemort who is so possessed by power and who cannot love, and who is indifferent to others' desires and devotion, it just doesn't add up. I could have accepted if they made her a child of Bellatrix' who had inherited her mother's obsession with the Dark Lord. My boyfriend argued that Voldemort might want an heir, but I don't believe that either, because Voldemort wants to live forever and thus there is no reason for an heir . I stand by this and my claim that this would never have happened in a novel by JK. Therefore I have decided to pretend it didn't happen. Sorry. 
 The Time-Turner  plot has also received some hits from fans. Claims of inconsistencies and the likes. I agree that this is an example of plot points that seem far-fetched and over-the-top, but I also believe that JK could have worked wonders with this in an actual novel and I am still and of course bummed that this will not happen. However, theatre doesn't have much time and space to work with and this is already a 5 hour play in two parts! 
 Albus and Scorpius are the stars of this script/play and are both beautifully written and acted. The play itself was brilliant and entertaining and quite well done. The script falls a little flat without the actors, sets and effects to support it. Personally I don't think it should exist in book form, mainly because it will ruin this new story for many fans. But I also realise that those who cannot see the play would want to experience it in another form, and I would probably feel the same way if I hadn't been able to see it either. The play would get 5 stars from me, and the book gets 3. 
 All in all I have difficulties viewing it as a continuation of the books. To me it's more of an addition to the universe, much like Fantastic Beasts is going to be. 
 If you read all this, thank you! I realise it is quite long ;)

 The setup 
 Figure skater Matty Marcus is struggling to not only recover from a back injury but also his failure to medal at the last Olympic Games. A benefactor reaches out and offers him an opportunity to earn some serious money while continuing to heal and get back into competitive shape. He moves to Montana to house sit a home that has the handsome rancher, Rob Lovely, as a neighbor. 
 The issues 
 With Rob, the flamboyant Matty finds strength, courage and confidence to do what's necessary to prepare for the upcoming Olympics. He also learns how to be submissive in the bedroom, being able to relinquish control without losing himself. Even though their feelings are deepening towards each other, Matty's eventual departure looms over them as they struggle to come to terms with the probable end date for their relationship. And, Rob has a 12-year old son who shows promise as a skater with Matty's help, complicating an already tough dilemma. Winning an 
 Olympic medal and doing everything he can to reach that goal is Matty's primary goal. 
 What worked for me 
 Matty forced me out of my comfort zone with respect to m/m romances. He's effeminate, dresses outrageously and wears makeup, leaving no question as to his sexual orientation. I was unsure if I could connect with him and here was the power of the story. Matty had to not only excel in his skating but also overcome the judges (and others) stereotypical thinking about his style. I loved that he never felt compelled to change any aspect of his identity, with full awareness of what it might cost him and the reactions of those around him. Rob's embrace of all that was Matty and his patience with him made him so appealing. Their romance was at times sweet and always sensual. I loved their relationship, even when Matty made it difficult. He got under my skin and I ended up adoring him. 
 What was a challenge for me 
 Be forewarned that the sex is graphic, which doesn't really bother me normally but there were some dom/sub scenes that pushed me beyond my limits. I actually found myself skimming over some of the encounters as I found them confusing to the story. 
 The bottom line 
 I loved the story, the romance and the sometimes bratty Matty. It's my understanding that the author was channeling the Olympic skater Johnny Weir and this book helped me develop a new level of respect and appreciation for him. My perceptions were completely altered and that's pretty powerful. I'm thrilled that the author created Matty and wrapped this wonderful story around him.

[FROM THE PREFACE:] 
 The Discworld is not a coherent fantasy world. Its geography is fuzzy, its chronology unreliable. A small traveling circle of firelight in a chilly infinity has turned out to be the home of defiant jokes and last chances. 
 There are no maps. You can't map a sense of humor. Anyway, what is a fantasy map but a space beyond which There Be Dragons? On the Discworld we know that There Be Dragons Everywhere. They might not all have scales and forked tongues, but they Be Here all right, grinning and jostling and trying to sell you souvenirs. 
 Enjoy. 
 Thus begins my Grand Discworld Reread, which will likely wreck my really great author gender ratio this year, although I'm not planning on reading them all in one fell swoop. This series is really near and dear to my heart -- I read every single book and grew up on them, devouring them from our school library, and I spent so many hours in Discworld MUD. I love this world so much. 
 However, this book is really not the best. I tell every new reader not to start with The Colour of Magic, and to pick up something like Guards! Guards! or Equal Rites instead -- partially because I overall prefer the Watch and the witches sub-series, but also because it takes Pratchett a little while to find his stride, his voice, his style. In this very earliest book, you can really see the nuts & bolts of him first figuring out how this lifelong series will work. 
 Still, though, I'm going to be stubborn and go through all 41 books in publication order, because I'm interested to follow a) the social and technological development within the Discworld itself, and b) the evolution of Pterry's writing as he goes. 
 The good: Ankh-Morpork is already fantastic. The best parts of this book imo are the first half within the city itself; it already has a living breathing identity of its own, and the comedy of Twoflower's oblivious arrival was great. 
 I really like the themes of technology vs. magic: part of the joy in this series is seeing how they replicate modern technological inventions but with magic. Rincewind, on the other hand, expresses his despair that he lives in such an absolutely bonkers world where science doesn't stand a chance. 
 Rincewind, Twoflower, and the Luggage (shush, it totally counts) are a good set of characters. They're classic, although Rincewind does more interesting things later; again, this book is testing the waters. But 'the first-ever tourist' as a plot is a fantastic conceit for showing off the Disc, and Twoflower is endearingly naive and cheerful as he waltzes his way from mortal peril to mortal peril, trailed by the cowering fake wizard. Also his ruminations about going everywhere & seeing everything just made me go yes, considering my love of seeing new places and how I wish I had all the money to just travel. 
 This book mainly spoofs things like Hercules/Conan-esque barbarian fantasy, magic swords, and Lovecraftian horrors. 
 For an old-time reader, the signs that Pterry has still not quite worked out his formula: 
 This is more like a collection of short stories assembled into the vague shape of a novel, just episodic adventures, rather than a single coherent story. Plotlines and characters are picked up and dropped in order to get on to the next sight, the next shenanigans. 
 The Patrician is unnamed, and not quite as cool as he becomes later, though you can see glimpses of it. 
 Death is really, really out-of-character for what I remember of him. Every time he expressed delight in random killing or lost his temperI was like :( :( considering my memories of the sympathetic, philosophical, sort-of-hero we grow to love later. 
 There aren't any named characters from the Watch yet. 
 There are like no female characters; the only one is a barely sketched-out outline of a stereotype, unlike his later strong female characters who bust out of their tropes. 
 There's only one footnote!! This especially caught me off-guard, considering Discworld is known for being rife with footnote humour. 
 That modern-day AU sequence is bizarre. I had completely forgotten about it. I was not a fan. 
 In conclusion tho: If you're a new reader, I still stick by my original advice: this is not the place to begin Discworld. The Colour of Magic is more interesting as an artefact of its time, as an archaeological fossil to this legendary series. If you are a stubborn completionist like me, just be prepared for the fact that this one is sloppy and messy and a little mediocre (around 2.5-3 stars from me)... but the series gets better (so, so so so so much better) later, and you should absolutely stick with it. This one is an interesting ride that briefly introduces you to this zany world, but nothing much of significance happens.

"Newark was left behind and the post-chaise-and-four entered on a stretch of flat country which offered little to attract the eye, or occasion remark." 
 Georgette Heyer was a wonderful writer. A beloved writer, in fact, known for her regency romances in particular. Her books are rich in detail--but not in a burdening, cumbersome way. And her characters are always nicely drawn from human nature--flaws abound, but that's always a good thing. Vices and temptations abound in her works--drinking, gambling (be it at the gaming table or in a sporting arena), keeping bad company, and fashion to name just a few examples. (How is fashion a vice? Well, if you're too vain or selfish and spend too much time primping in front of a mirror, then chances are you're in for a comeuppance. Also, spending too much money on fashion--clothes, hats, gloves, jewelry, etc.--is just one way it can be a vice.) 
 In Regency Buck, we've got the story of a brother and sister newly arrived in London. Peregrine Tavener, the brother, and his older sister, Judith Tavener. They are coming to set up house, and perhaps even more importantly to meet their guardian. (Both of their parents have died. And the father's will left them under the care of Lord Worth.) They are expecting an older gentleman. A man that would have been the contemporary of their father. Someone with gout presumably. What they find is that Lord Worth is a young man--just a handful of years older. He isn't particularly pleased with this added responsibility, and he's not shy admitting this to his wards. But for one year at least--until Judith's birthday--Lord Worth is their official guardian. 
 The Taveners do set up their own house. Mrs. Scattergood, a relation (cousin???) of Lord Worth, is Judith's companion. Needed during that time to protect young women and provide them with counsel on how to behave in society. An older woman to act as chaperone. Of course, Peregrine, offers protection to his sister as well. But who's protecting him? Peregrine being prone to gambling and partying. When Peregrine becomes engaged to a young woman, Harriet, then a few strange coicidences occur to threaten his life which convinces Worth that someone is out to kill his ward. 
 The two stand to inherit much money when they come of age. And for this reason, suitors abound for Judith's hand. One of her most persistent suitors is her cousin, Bernard Tavener. But Lord Worth turns them all away. Saying that no man will marry her while he is still her guardian. Something that both repulses and pleases her. She's known some of the men are completely unsuitable--some as old as her father, all looking for a wealthy wife--but the idea of being controlled by a man irritates her at the same time. 
 Worth (Julian) and Judith (whom he persists in calling Clorinda) are always bickering. The banter flows easily between these two. While both tend to be a bit cranky around the other, the reader knows without any doubts that these two secretly feel very differently about each other. 
 I love Worth and Judith. I love the rich-layers of Regency Buck as well. For example, Judith's reading of Sense and Sensibility. And the presence of Lord Byron and the discussion of his poetry. There are a dozen or so other things I could point out, but those are just two examples of bits that made me smile.

Oh god. I'm going to say a lot of things because I just finished this and I don't know if any of them will be coherent. I think, I think this is somewhere between 3.5 and 3.75 stars. But maybe I'll save it at three, because there is just... there is so much. And I don't know what or how to think. 
 My short review is: This is the best novel Handler has written (as Handler) since The Basic Eight. I love Adverbs, but I don't quite count that as a novel; if you know me, you'll know that I was NOT ENAMOURED with Why We Broke Up and I DNF the incest book that I pretend doesn't exist (because god, why, why, why was that written. why did that need to be written). The prose remains Handlerian--Handler is a stylist, I get it, he has a huge crush on Nabokov (and why shouldn't he)--but at the same time, it's toned down. One of the reasons I couldn't stand WWBU was because of how pretentious it felt, except for the giant paragraph at the end where Min says everything she isn't. I know him well enough to spot the hallmarks of his style ("I thought," he said, "that I said that"; not a direct quote but he does have a habit of putting his dialogue tags in strange places in the dialogue, so you've got to wait for it), but at the same time, they weren't overwhelming. They didn't distract from the story. 
 I've gotta say one thing on language, though. Let's talk about race, Daniel. Let's talk about some of the weird stuff you have in here that, frankly, I don't know how it made it in. Especially after the National Book Awards. You made a good apology, you put your money where your mouth was, and you didn't phrase it as "sorry if you were offended"--it was legitimately "sorry I said a racist thing." But? But? A woman "screamed the way the appearance of a black man makes everything suddenly scary." What the actual christ, Daniel. Yes, Manny is black, yes, he shows up, yes, the woman screams because of piracy, but just... dear lord. I hate that sentence. There are a few others, a strange comment about (black) police officers working "twice as hard, due to injustice,"one about a "knocking, clasping ritual believed at the time to be favoured by black people," and there's one other. The first sentence I've mentioned is absolutely not okay, and it bothered me throughout. The others were just... strange. They felt unnecessary. Unneeded. Why did you put those in there, Daniel? Why? 
 Okay. Now to the actual plot of the book: 
 The basic plot is there's a dad who's in radio and he's floundering in life. His infinitely more interesting daughter, Gwen, has been caught stealing. As punishment, she's has to go to an old folks home and talk to old people there. Suddenly, piracy happens. And we watch that unfold. 
 Interesting plot. I found this a really gripping story, and I had to keep reading to find out what would happen next. 
 Character-building was weird. I didn't like Phil a whole lot; he's kind of a sleazebucket and I never quite trusted him. Yet he shares equal screen-time with his daughter, Gwen. I found myself less interested in Phil's parts, partially because I had a hard time following what was happening, but also because he reads as a terrible person. I don't quite know if he's supposed to be sympathetic. Part of me doesn't think he is, mainly because of the way he treats Levine and ignores Marina, HIS WIFE, and is a bit of a snooper. See also: him reading Levine's personal file on her computer, where she's writing an erotic note, and he Gets Ideas . On the other hand, he's billed first on the book blurb, so he's clearly one of the protagonists. No doubt he's flawed, and I really don't mind flawed protagonists, but on the whole he turned out kind of bleh. 
 Gwen, though. Gwen's intriguing. Fourteen-year-old who's frustrated with everything, alter-ego who commits crimes, suddenly swept up in ideas of piracy? Yes, that's more like it. To be honest, I found myself wishing this were more overtly her story, rather than flipping back and forth between the two. I felt bad for Phil once or twice (when Gwen goes missing, but that was more regarding the horror of a missing child ) but Gwen I sympathized more with. This isn't because I read a lot of YA, although maybe it is--she was just more interesting overall. 
 As for other characters: they didn't feel as defined. In some, that's okay. In some, that's not. I wanted more Marina, Phil's wife, Gwen's mum--she intrigued me more than her husband did. The Glassermans were occasionally sketchy, although I was okay with that. Amber was fascinating, perhaps a little thin but nonetheless amusing. I also thought this was going to be a tale of reconciliation between Gwen and Naomi, and I never quite got why Gwen broke off her friendship with Naomi. Oh well. Can't win 'em all.  
 As for the actual piracy: Okay. I should've seen bloodshed coming, but I was absolutely shocked that Gwen was prepared to kill. That's such a drastic action, especially for a fourteen-year-old. Yes, I've read TBE, I know Handler writes this grand tradition of teenage murderesses, but also, that's... that's so big... and it didn't ring true, not quite, not for me. I also didn't get Gwen's sudden PIRACY!!! obsession. It happens as soon as she meets Errol, but I really would've loved to watch it expand. It felt, eh, not quite shoe-horned in, but dealt with too quickly. There was a lot that worked, a lot that didn't. Eh.  
 Oh, and there's a twist at the end that makes you want to re-read the book. I guess I should've seen it coming that Gwen and Errol were related, that Errol was grandfather, that he would die, but I didn't. Don't know how I felt about it, although I didn't feel like it was a cheapo plot device. So that's good.  
 Aaaaaand one last thing that I loved: I shipped Gwen/Amber all the way through and then they KISS on the BOAT and it's described as ROMANTIC and it was actually pretty glorious. SO THAT WAS REALLY NICE.  
 OVERALL: I don't regret reading this, I had a lot of fun with it, although it's less of a fun romp than I would've liked. Be prepared for strangeness and terror and feelings.

The POV changes a lot and I can see what the author was trying to do but I found that the voices blended together too much and she would head- hop even within a scene so there was more confusion over who was owning a scene than there should have been. So, the novel: 
 It's 2011 and it's the end of the world in just a few short days- there's an asteroid on its way, one large enough to destroy everything. There's a ship, a small one, that can take 80 people and potentially save their lives. 
 Sh*t gets real fast. Although the narrative is written for maybe a grade six level, I think the contents are more appropriate for an older age group. 
 It's bleak, it's hopeless, and I loved that for this novel. It should be depressing- the entire world is ending and so many people are going to die. The only survivors are going to be eighty people from the US, which is problematic for so many reasons that I can't even get into it. 
 I hate how the character of Essence is treated and even Cordelia. Please, people. Women are people too, I promise. The Yago guy is creepy and I'd be happy not to see him again. Of course, that probably means that he's going to live for ever. 
 I disliked the sheer number of foolish names in this novel- what is wrong with the name you were born with? They all give themselves nicknames because they obviously don't understand that it doesn't work like that. 
 This novel is way over populated by white blond(e) people, but that's pretty much par for the course in media today. The only people of colour are either 'disfigured' or are the creepy serial killer to be: Yago. 
 The plot moves along at a nice pace and the destruction of the Earth was nice- I kept thinking, nice, K.A. actually did it. 
  
 All that said, I'm going to be reading the next book in the series.

Review for Alpha by Jasinda Wilder 
 Wow. 
 Just wow. 
 No, really, that's all I've got. 
 Alpha by Jasinda Wilder is by far the HOTTEST book I have read so far in 2014. It is going to take an act of God or some other monumental occurrence for anyone to top it. This is the first book of the year that I have read and the moment I finished it I wanted to skip right back to the beginning and start again. I rarely, if ever, reread a book. I just don't have time and frankly there are just so many out there that I find myself moving on quickly. Alpha is going to be joining my short list of go-to books when I'm in a book slump. 
 If you haven't ever read a book by Jasinda Wilder before, well, you need to pick this one up. I can't even find the right words to explain how completely amazing this book is. Not just the storyline, which wasn't exactly what I expected, I LOVE when an author can blow through my expectations and leave me on the other side slack-jawed, but the characters in this book -- so fully developed I swear somewhere in the world there just HAS to live a Kyrie and Roth. That's how much those two got into my head. 
 Okay, into the story we go (no spoilers as always whores)... 
 Kyrie is having a bad time. Her boss is a douche canoe. Her job was just made obsolete. Her mother is crazy. Her bills are stacked up beyond anything she can ever get out from under and then she gets a check. Not just any check. It's ten grand... should she cash it? The choice is simple... cash it and avoid becoming homeless. The checks kept coming. Every month, for a year... and then it's time to repay her debt. 
 Roth is a mystery. He's private and reclusive. Sex on a freakin' stick. Kyrie describes him best... 
 "He was totally dominant, powerful and confident, skilled and passionate and attentive." 
 I've read dozens of the dominant millionaire meets poor girl books. The men are almost always overbearing, overprotective, jackholes... they can be sweet and sexy, but overall in reality if anyone were to treat a woman like that we would run... run far and fast and not look back. Roth... oh man... Roth is THE KING of all millionaire (or billionaire) alpha men. He's bossy, but with purpose. He is protective, but not smothering. He is courteous and would do absolutely anything for those he cares for. Oh and sexy... can't forget sexy. Wait, did I mention his dirty mouth? Wow. 
 "That's my girl... I love the way you take my cockadoodledoo, Kyrie. You take it all, and you always want more. Sofa king hot."

 Move over Christian, Jesse, and Gideon... Roth is taking no prisoners and making you all look like bumbling teenagers. 
 FIVE PLUS STARS for an amazing storyline and FIVE PLUS drenched, torn, and stuffed in a pocket panties for the best smut of 2014. Absolute MUST READ NOW.

I thought this was the best Laundry book yet, and judging by average Goodreads reviews, the public agrees with me. So let's see if I can justify my opinion. 
 I think a good portion of it is finding a way to incorporate vampire myths into a Cthulhu cosmology, which not even Call of Cthulhu has ever really done well. It's not a curse or a virus or anything--it's a symbiote that's attracted to ritual magic, and it provides its host with superior physical abilities; an immunity to K Syndrome, thus allowing them to use magic without inevitably killing themselves; immortality; and mind control. Sure, they need to drink blood and burn in the sun, but, well, there's no such thing as a free lunch. 
 As it turns out, it's not just ritual magic, it's a specific frame of mind that can often come about through ritual magic, and when a group of quantitative analysts end up investigating a new means of market prediction that ends up attracting the parasites (vampires-as-bankers is obvious, but I still appreciated it), it's up for the Laundry to deal with the problem. Bureaucratically, of course. 
 That was probably my favorite part of the novel, actually. When Bob went on a mission to the bank, I was fully expecting the vampires to capture him, to rant at him for a while, and then for the cavalry to come in and plot to get resolved, because that's how the previous Laundry books have tended to go. Essentially, I was expecting the spy thriller part of the book to win out. But what actually happened was that the plodding bureaucracy part won out, and that's when I paused, noticed how much of the book was left, and wondered where the plot was going next. 
 I also liked The Rhesus Chart's version of vampire society--namely, that there isn't one. Most vampires who survive any length of time are sociopaths who are willing to go to nearly any length to avoid being discovered, since burning to death in sunlight is obviously an easy weakness to exploit. Every other vampire is a threat to their own existence because it increases the chances of discovery. As such, the ideal number of vampires in any given area is one and existing vampires enforce this with extreme prejudice. 
 The biggest problem with The Rhesus Chart is the increasing density of memes. I get that self-awareness is a part of the Laundry, and part of the reason the vampire bankers were interesting early on is that their first reaction was immediately: "How does this work? Sunlight? Stakes? Garlic? Blood? Consecrated ground? What are we dealing with here?" but when you're literally quoting "If I fits, I sits," it does a lot more to take me out of the novel than to ground me in Bob's character. I get it. He's the nerdy IT consultant dealing with Lovecraftian horrors. That is, in fact, the basis for the whole series, and I don't need it constantly in my face to remember it. 
 Well, or maybe it's the tendency of Howard to interject himself into the narrative to exposition-dump. I do love worldbuilding and normally this wouldn't bother me, but it's mostly in the form of bureaucratic reports, and dry memos are dry even in a fictional context. 
 Oh, and the mention that the CASE NIGHTMARE GREEN awareness campaign could be:Disguised as background material for a role-playing game if it leaks early and we need plausible deniability.I see what you did there, Stross 
 The resolution bothered me as well: Namely, the fact that Basil was the mole. I figured it out as soon as he showed up in the meeting, since he was clearly trying too hard to be the out-of-touch pensioner who's completely harmless and who everyone can safely ignore. I can't actually complain about this, because it's the most reasonable course of action for a vampire hiding at the heart of an organization explicitly tasked to deal with that sort of threat. But I knew it was going to happen, and after the way hiring on the Scrum threw me, it was a bit of a letdown.  
 I went into The Rhesus Chart a bit disappointed the Stross wasn't pulling the trigger on CASE NIGHTMARE GREEN, but after the way it turned out, I can forgive him. Hopefully future Laundry books are more like this one and less like the previous books in the series.

Aaaaaah look, overall, this book delivered what I'd expected. It surprised me in a few places, skirting around issues that I thought it'd have (the love cures mental illness trope) with ease, and delighted me in others (the family!!). But it never really came together in the way it sort of promised it might... 
 I was very worried, going into this, that it was going to be one of those "girl has genuine problems until her love for a new boy solves everything" books. You know, that super relatable and realistic story that's not even a little infuriating... And of course, the whole premise of this book does set it up a little unavoidably, so I was aware that I was going to cringe a little. In the end, I only picked it up because I kept seeing it at the library and remembering all the good reviews. I guess they weren't for nothing. 
 The problem was the romance itself. Because its like we were given a few corner pieces of a puzzle and then expected to believe that suddenly that was an entire picture. (I feel like that simile got away from me in the middle there, but it's the best way I can word it right now) The characters weren't bad? Linus was a sweet outline of a character, and Audrey was relatable (well okay to fourteen year old me, and also anxiety/lizard brain me but.... still points), but there was no chemistry. Or at least, no on page chemistry. 
 I mean, don't get me wrong I thought the notes were cute, and the nicknames and the games... but there's not really any reason for Linus to care so much. I could understand curiosity, but he has a crush without any real motivation for one, given that their talking is limited quite severely. He only met her once before, so it's not even like he remembers who she is outside of the anxiety. I guess it's just you're not shown what would make this random teenage boy be anything more than just polite to his best friend's sister, especially given that she runs and hides every time he comes near at first. 
 And then later we're expected to believe they're in love?? I mean obviously we're talking high school love, but still... they keep talking about all these texts and these hang outs... but all we're shown are these challenges. Don't get me wrong, they're super cute! I just find it hard to take it from quirky dares to somehow they know and trust each other so much....  
 This would have bugged me a lot more, if not for the fact that Audrey's family takes up so much of the book. Felix was honestly such a gift of a character. Having a much younger brother myself, I could relate so much to the kinda shift in dynamics with an age gap like that, and the antics of little kids. Honestly his contributions were so spot on, and so funny. He reminded me a lot of my little brother.... maybe that's why I'm so soft on him. 
 Audrey's parents were a little over the top... but I found it more funny than annoying. I think I really appreciate antics in a book (like the argument with the siblings over Shreddies, and the mum's obsession with daily mail and everything that caused). It adds a lot of life to the book and, though it's kinda exaggerated to make it interesting, it hits a little closer to the truth. That sort of chaos is what families are like, or at least what my experience of them has been like (especially ones with lots of kids ahaha) . 
 The final thing that I really enjoyed about this book was the portrayal of anxiety. What I liked most was those ups, amidst the downs, because that is something often missed by authors writing about anxiety. It's too easy to write panic on edge all the time, but that's not what it's like. There's periods of it going away, and you thinking its gone, and then it can come back in manageable ways and overwhelming ways, and it's not often that books really show all of this at once.  I also liked the sort of techniques she used, and the relationship she had with her counsellor. Well, save the whole going off her meds thing. But that was also another really well done plot, because I feel like that feeling good and stopping medication is so common, and that delay between her choice and the consequences was crucial.  
 I feel like I would have enjoyed this book more if I'd just had more?? More details, more feelings, I guess? I'm not sure. It wasn't a a bad book, though. A good thing to read between assignments to clear my head a little...

Riley tries to catch a demon in the school library but when something doesn't feel right and it all goes wrong she's left humliated. Switching to Beck's point of view Paul's apprentice it follow them both on a hunt but when things take a tragic turn and Paul Blackthorne is killed, it's left to Beck to break the new to Riley. Devestated Riley is now all on her own, fending for herself which pushes her more into Trapping to make some money, the rest of the book follows her journey of dealing with her fathers death, trying to be a demon trapper and falling in love for the first time... 
 I will be honest, I was quite dissapointed with Forsaken,

 So I sit down and start to read and it's starts off good, some action, a back story so I know who all the characters are but as it moves on, especially after Paul's death the book goes way down, gone are they demons and the book becomes more about Riley dealing with having no parents and trying to look after herself, there were a few incidents which brings the book more entertainment but it goes sour too quickly for me. 
 Only at the end did it start to pick up again with a major fight between Trappers and Demons and to be honest I didn't think the ending was all that great either. 
 I was torn between giving the book 2 or 3 stars, in the end I decided 3 because I liked Riley and the action that eventually appeared in the book. 
 I won't rush to read Forbidden but I would like to give it a try and hope that it's better and to continue on with the story.

I could enjoy this book better than the first one for various reasons. I was more prepared for the whole concept of getting from bad to worse to devastating. In Life As We Know It, Miranda sees people once in a while but Alex can't help but see people (dead or alive) when he walks to school or does his rounds.

 I want Curt to know he caused the death of that girl behind the wall so he can feel guilty. It's a better punishment than jail, in my opinion.

As much as I enjoy the Percy Jackson series, this new series featuring brother and sister Carter and Sadie is even richer and more edge-of-your-seat. The shifting point of view between the two siblings (and their snarky sibling-esque asides to each other) work beautifully, and Riordan breathes life into the well-known and little-known Egyptian gods in a way that he never quite achieves with the Olympians. A captivating and multi-layered story... can't wait to see what he does with the sequel.

Picked up Trinity War on a recommendation after posting an interest in Forever Evil. I can see why this is probably required reading for anybody interested in trying on John's next big book. This does come off a little like an extended prologue to Geoff's Forever Evil. Have a few friends (Anne's review , Mike's review) with dramatically different opinions about this one and I sort of fall in the middle I guess. 
 I wasn't sold on Pandora. She is a central figure in this one and I just never bought into her or her curse. I feel like Johns, Lemire, and Fawkes could have put this together somehow without needing to introduce a new character. The "magic" thing has just never really done it for me. A little here and there is just fine, but it's really a big part of this collection. Probably why this version of the Question bugged me too. Not enough Rorshach and too much Harry Potter in his back story. Could have done without the trip to Heaven or purgatory or whatever. Again with the magic, spirits, and angels. I like Constantine. Just not mixed with my Batman. This is why I never had an interest in the Justice League Dark title. I was also a little unclear as to why everybody wanted to kick each other's ass at the end. I was never really sure if it was me or that the time line between the different titles collected was disjointed and didn't flow smoothly. 
 I did like seeing Superman lose it. The back and forth between Waller's League and the original League amused. For some reason this collection reminded me of Identity Crisis (which I liked) at times. Maybe because of the mystery angle or the big reveal at the end  the tiny woman did it . Despite not being a "magic" fan, it was fun seeing Shazam and Constantine hanging out together at a bar. Diana and Steve's awkward " we're ex's" exchange. This one definitely had a couple of moments I enjoyed. I also liked most of the artwork in this one too. Ivan Reis and Doug Mahnke put together some good stuff here. 
 Awkward. 
 I have to say it pulled together for me at the very end and left me excited to check out Forever Evil.  Bring on the Crime Syndicate!  I really think that this was the intent from the beginning of this story. I just think they could have done this without this mammoth crossover, confusing story, and the Trinity of Sin stuff. This is a case where less probably would have been more for me.
