The first of Block's books I didn't fall into and float around wrapped in bliss. This is a collection of re-told fairy tales, and the only one I really liked was "Wolf". That story had everything I adore about Block's writing- the perfect adolescent girl voice, the atmospheric prose, the hint of danger and dispair- but the others left me cold.

Holden Caulfield is one of those characters that lives in the immagination of a lot of people. A young man unsure of his place in the world, not really trying to fit in and struggling with his feelings of being rootless and aimless. This is a snapshot of a few days in his life, the people he interacts with and his attitude to them. He is a sorry character, but I could see reflections of my own life in his. 
 I would probably have enjoyed this more as a teenager but I really disliked those years so a revisit is a bit torturous.
Good use of a format I normally find stale: letters. The characters are wonderfully written, brilliant people who aren't normal in the slightest. The plot is unreal and not ordinary. Fun to read.

This long book is worth the investment. There are endearing characters who are developed well, and a realistic plot that progresses slowly over time. The setting of this book isn't one I normally take interest in, but I'm glad all the hype surrounding this a few years back caused me to finally pick it up.

"The dead appear to us in dreams, because that's the only way they can make us see them; what we see us only a projection, beamed from a great distance, light shining at us from a dead star..." 
 It feels like it took me a year to read this book but I don't mind. I really did enjoy it... but don't know why. I hated all the characters, but liked them at the same time!

This may just be y favorite book out of the slew of fiction I've read this year. It's a juxtaposed tale of a Harvard grad student in the midst of her dissertation research set against the events surrounding the Salem witch trials in 1692. As you might expect, the two stories end up intertwining, but that is by no means a criticism. 
 This is a warm, beautifully crafted story, and the texture of Connie's world is very believable to me in a way that dreamy, detail-oriented narratives are to sentimentalists and dreamers. It's a story about a lot of things including the power of women, the hysteria of crowds, the place of people within a natural order, and most of all, family and all that entails.
A very good book with some disturbing themes. Both compelling and uncomfortable.

A magical anthology with some real gems; perfect for younger audiences and those wishing for less horrible things than is found in more contemporary collections. Gabriel-Ernest by Saki and Come Lady Death by Peter S. Beagle may have been my favorites. The title pages feature delightful illustrations, which is a nice bonus.
Then cliffhangers though...

Not for me..... I rarely gravitate towards Romances but a friend insisted I give this a try but nope, still not a fan of romance books and I don't think I ever will. 
 PS Just to clarify I like romance in my books but I find that books centered around the romance not my cup of tea.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Wow. The only thing I'm a bit torn about is the back story thing. Does it take or add to this particular telling? Certainly one of the most terrifying aspects about this character is the uncertainty behind "his" back story. Nevertheless, I think the way it was told, and the comment at the end about how the story changes every time, might be enough to suggest this is ONE OF THE MANY. I prefer to think it as that, and keep the chilling and thrilling emotions this masterpiece brought to the table. By the way, the new coloring must be the impression you get of this if you're reading it for the first time anywhere after 2008. Then you can go back to read the original, but this coloring just adds too much to it.

The synopsis pretty much sums up this book, and indeed, Saving Cee Cee Honeycutt is a heartwarming, entertaining story about a neglected little girl who found love in places and people she could never imagine. 
 I warmed up to the character Cecelia Rose Honeycutt from the very begging. Being merely twelve years old, she is burdened with the task of taking care of her mentally-ill mother who dreams of a glorious life which has long-passed. Her father is always running away from harsh realities of life by using his job as an excuse, and Mrs. Odell is her only refuge. 
 After her mother's sudden death, Cee Cee moves in to stay with her great aunt Tootie. The first person she gets to know besides her aunt is none other than Aunt Tootie's personal cook, Oletta Jones. At the beginning, Oletta is cold towards Cee Cee, but after knowing her past, she sympathizes Cee Cee's plight and offers the child her support. 
 Cee Cee quickly learns that the women in the neighbourhood are kind, though each of them have different personalities. Aunt Tootie is always optimistic, Oletta Jones has a warm heart beneath her cool behaviour, Miz Goodpepper is nice but somewhat quirky, and Miz Hobbs' presence always makes her uneasy. 
 Jam-packed with wit, humour and charm - spiced up by the presence of two quirky, eccentric, always-at-each-other's-throats neighbours - Miz Goodpepper and Miz Hobbs, Saving Cee Cee Honeycutt will definitely make its way into your heart.
I loved this book, and thought it was a really fun read. One of the better young adult books I've read this year!

ARRGGHHHHHH!!! This book is incredible! It was such a beautiful story, and it was so well written, and the characters were great... I could go on and on about this book (And I am about to do just that!) I don't think that this review will do the book justice, and I don't even know if it will be cohesive enough to make sense, but I loved this book so much and highly recommend it! 
 The story is written in short, punchy chapters that makes it a quick easy read (in contrast to the content being handled). Some parts of the story are beautiful and poetic, whilst others are gruesome and tragic. The different themes and moods are well balanced, and the story is very well written. 
 The story alternated between four characters' points of view, all written in first person. At first I was wary of this style, but I thought that it really added to the story and helped it to flow. The different characters all have different backgrounds and experiences which change the way they experience events. It was fascinating to learn about how different people viewed the events, and there is such a brilliantly wide range of characters that made the story so much better! 
 Joana: "Guilt is a hunter" 
 Joana is the first character introduced to the story. She is a Lithuanian nurse with a big heart to hep other people. She is my favourite of the main characters; her resilience and determination really stand out and she soldiers on regardless of the difficult circumstances. She has a caring, loving nature which, when coupled with her courage, makes her a really great character. 
 Florian: "Fate is a hunter" 
 Florian is the next character introduced, and he is probably the most complex. A young Prussian hiding secrets, he can be prickly and grumpy at times. However, once you get to know him better he can be quite compassionate and it is fascinating to read from his perspective and get to better understand his views on what is happening. There are times when he is selfish, but also times when he is so selfless that he seems almost like a different person. Just when you think you have Florian figured out, you'll have a new piece of information sprung on you and be fascinated by him all over again. 
 Emilia: "Shame is a hunter" 
 Emilia is a Polish girl, only fifteen years old. Joana is my favourite main character, but Emilia is my favourite perspective to read from. Despite her youth, she understands much of what is going on around her, although there are times when it really stands out that she is only just still a young girl. She puts on a brave face and keeps going on, despite everything that is going on around her, and it was definitely a unique perspective on the events. 
 Alfred: "Fear is a hunter" 
 Alfred. Where to start. Every review I've read about this book said that Alfred was the worst thing that happened in the story and that they hated him. Whilst I also immensely disliked him, I am glad that his perspective was included because it gives significant insight into the situation. When you look past the initial dislike, I think the next thing you feel for Alfred is pity. If only he would open his eyes and look at the people around him! It doesn't excuse the things he did, but nonetheless I think that more than anything I feel sorry for Alfred, and his lack of understanding about what he was doing and the real motives of the people around him. 
 Klaus: 
 Klaus was not a main character, but he definitely deserves a mention. He is small and innocent, yet has some unexpected insight. He knows enough to go along with the stories which the others have created to keep them safe, and I am very glad that he was included. 
 Ingrid: 
 Ingrid was not a major character, but she deserves a mention. I love her so much! She is brave, bold, determined, kind, and doesn't let her blindness stop her. 
 Shoe Poet: 
 Look, I think you can tell just how much I love this book by the fact that I'm obsessing over the shoe poet Heinz. But please bear with me, he was my most favourite character in the whole book! He is extremely wise, he is loving and caring (particularly towards Klaus, and also Emilia) and he is also honest. Also known as Opi, the shoe poet has endured hardship and sets his eyes on the future. He is brilliant. Alhfg;hldfg;mhuns; I love him so much I can't even!!! 
 Um, so yeah the characters were brilliant. But also, the messages which were conveyed through the book were meaningful, important and included into the story fantastically. The way the characters endure hardship, the sacrifices they make for each other, the way that they show kindness and love even in the dark times. Despite the underlying tragedy and horrifying circumstances it is a really beautiful story. 
 This review was not intended to be this long, but I loved so many things about it that I just had to go into details about all of them. I don't feel my review really encapsulates the novel or does it justice, but it is a great story and I highly recommend it!

A book about a girl who keeps dying and then reliving her life over again. Usually I like plots like that, but I never got a good grasp for "the rules" of the setup. Sometimes she remembers parts of her life, sometimes she doesn't? The book was too slow moving for me. I liked the sections in which she dies repeatedly over the course of multiple short chapters while she attempts to overcome a particular deadly obstacle. The long periods of her life bored me because I didn't really feel invested in any of the characters. I put the book down at about 70% complete and I just struggled to pick it back up again (but eventually did just to say I finished it).

I'll admit that I picked up this book to read because Stephen Colbert recommended it. It was well-written, with interesting characters. But the plot rambled on a bit and the story seemed incomplete. 
 The US had gone downhill. The rich are holed up in private communities. Dangerous gangs roam about. So Cal and Frida head off into the woods. 
 The story unfolds, slowly revealing their past and moving them forward. But the danger and mystery seem incomplete. I had higher hopes for how the story would go.

Ultimately I had to give this book 3 stars. Mainly because it felt like I was reading two different books here. One where Sarah was struggling with her sexuality, and the other with battle sequences. 
 I typically avoid urban fantasy, because the love interests tend to be a little bit rapey. I thought with a lesbian protagonist I'd avoid that trope. And while the love interest is fine, there's a sequence in the middle of the book that bothered me, involving the heroine and two men that didn't ring true. Of course, it was all downhill from there. 
 So while I finished and did mostly enjoy this book, I won't be continuing in the series.

I liked the ideas in it and I always like reading about new concepts about "magic" in the fantasy world. It got slow around the end I found and it would pick up again in parts before going on a memory tangent. Still I'm enjoying the series so far so fingers crossed that I enjoy the rest.

I started this book in a very weird time for me : I've kind of lost all interest in contemporary romance novels. I feel like I've read a lot of them, and they're pretty much the same (yeah I know, that's a depressing analysis). I read blurbs, and feel like I've already read the book. So yeah, that's pretty much my mood lately : 
 (But hey don't leave it's gonna get better, I promise!) 
 I love Kyla's writing but I'm generally more familiar with her fantasy series The Affiliate (if you haven't read it yet, by the way, do read this series, it's great!) 
 Anyway... I'm following Kyla on Facebook, and I love reading what she posts during the process of writing her books. And she was so convincing that Austin and Julia were something else, that she started to wake the once avid romance reader still living somewhere inside me. I signed up for the chance to read it early, and here I am! 
 And let me tell you that for the first time in what seems a while, I loved a romance book from beginning to end! 
 Austin and Julia... they were hot (like really really hot), feisty, everyhting I needed. 
 This book has it all! It's sexy, intense, but mostly... full of feelings. It made me FEEL so much emotions! It dealt with a lot of subjects, which I won't enumarate because it could be considered as spoilers, but the thing is... in many books, a lot of issues are added just for the purpose of plot, and are not handled realistically. In this story, K.A. Linde does not use those tricks, she deals with the character's issues with a real honesty, and I absolutely loved it. 
 The Wright Mistake is my favorite book in the series so far. 
 And this is me after reading the book :
I read this in 6th grade for a book report... Haunting is the only way to describe it.

I was struggling to decide whether to give this 4 or 5 stars, but ultimately I decided on 5. I know if I had read this closer to the time read the previous books there would have been no question. I wasn't so attached to the characters anymore because it's been forever since I read the first two book and I think that is understandable. I'm still pretty much basing the rating on enjoyment (as if I didn't always do that) and even though there were things I didn't like in this book I still really enjoyed it. 
 This book had so many elements that I like: great main characters, action, science fiction, mystery, romance etc. It was great to see Amy and Elder discussing and making decisions together and collecting pieces to see what's really going on. I loved learning more and more and figuring it all out even though it was pretty easy to guess who the real enemy is. *Haymitch voice* This once again showed how ruthless and careless humans can be. And the sad thing? It didn't surprise me at all.  
 The one thing that irritated me was Amy's dad (and maybe some other "Earthborns"). That attitude! First he didn't like Elder. He didn't like the "shipborns" and he treated them like he and the Earthborns were better than them. Then all he wanted was blood. To kill all the aliens. Basically every human thought of Centauri-Earth as their planet and thought they could do anything without consequences. But no, it's not their world, it's already inhabited. 
 Yes, I do like conflict. Otherwise I couldn't give this five stars! :D But I really liked how everything turned out in the end, I think it was a good way to end this trilogy.

I love William Herondale more than possibly any other character and it was the fact that he was in this story that I read it. 
 I didn't really understand the point of the story and the only reason I even gave it 3 stars was because of Will, Tessa, and James. Otherwise I felt like the characters didn't really act like themselves and everything was forced. The dialogue didn't seem realistic to Will and Tessa's characters. However it did kind of make me excited to see how James's story pans out!

This is probably a familiar story to many. I had meticulously planned an order in which to whittle down my 'To-Read' pile, including books from my 'must-reads' challenge. However, I work in a school and recently our library ordered a whole bunch of new books. Good new books. Not just ones that some stuffy old man has suggested is good reading for secondary school kids. Amongst these was Moira Young's Blood Red Road which has been on my list ever since I attended a talk with her and Michael Grant. With that in mind, Blood Red Road shoved every over book out of the line to stand smugly at the front. 
 To briefly summarise what to expect, think Mad Max with a young, female protagonist and a severe lack of cars. This is a dystopian, but felt quite refreshing after reading so many city-based, political dystopias over the last few years. The world is all heat and sand, with only a few idyllic, green areas surviving. People scavenge for parts to repair their homes and sandships and they survive by using the resources left behind by the ancestors they refer to as Wreckers. 
 Saba lives on the dried up lakebed of Silverlake with her Papa, twin brother Lugh and little sister Emmi. Their home, a tin hut held together by scraps, protects them from the harsh heat of the sun and the red dust storms which sweep across the desert. During one such storm, Saba and Lugh are caught in the middle of it, throwing themselves facedown in the sand to protect themselves. But four men arrive on horseback, grabbing Lugh, and galloping away as quickly as the storm arrived. 
 Saba's Papa dies as he attempts to retrieve Lugh, and she is left with the little sister she blames for their mother's death years before. The twins have never been apart before, and Saba promises that she'll do anything to get him back. She sets off for Hopetown seeking revenge and the brother she cannot live without. 
 In recent years there has been a real push for strong, female leads, and therefore, Saba's journey should feel refreshing. I quite liked that it was she, the quiet sibling who liked to remain in her brother's shadow, who was the one to set out and save her brother. However, there have been so many YA stories that have switched the 'damsel in distress' roles, that I didn't experience the same levels of anxiety as a result. 
 There's a point in the plot where Saba is forced to entertain the residents of Hopetown in a gladiator-style arena. Opponents fight each other until one is unable to continue, and when one fighter has lost three matches, they must run for freedom in the hope that the spectators will not kill them first. Saba is good, and quickly becomes famous. Her moniker as the 'Angel of Death' gains a lot of attention and sells many tickets. Yet, none of it felt real. Before the first match, I didn't feel we were given a real indication that Saba was capable of defending herself that well. Nothing from her history suggests she would make a good combat fighter, and it's almost like she's good only because the plot requires it of her. I needed a bit more realism here.  
 There were a few exciting twists and turns along the way, and the introduction of some fantastic characters. Some sequences of events were particularly clever - The escape from the slave pit was well executed and thought through  and as the story's events continued, I relaxed into it. It began a little coincidental, and a lot of things which should have had reasoning, didn't. For example, Saba's unique natural ability in close combat despite having no real explanation as to why. 
 Saba made for an interesting protagonist. At first, she is presented as the shadow to Lugh's light. It gives the impression that she is shy, doubts herself and that she looks to her brother for support. When he is taken, it's as if she has lost a limb. But, this severance also unleashes someone who is the complete opposite of the Saba in the first few pages. She is fierce, determined and is an excessively angry individual. And that is what characterises her throughout the whole novel; her anger. 
 Yes, she's been taught from a young age to distrust people but her immediate defence is to be angry and rude. This often leads her to treat her friends the same and, for the majority of the time, tends to cloud her judgment. Those people who are genuinely helpful are pushed away consistently, and it's a wonder how they never give up and leave. She is also incredibly guarded, taking the conscious effort to keep up her walls even when she is presented with powerful reasons to relax. 
 I also found her particularly masculine. Unfortunately, I felt as if Saba had fallen into the "strong, independent, YA female protagonist' trap where she came across masculine in order to appear strong. Most of her triumphs were successful as a result of violence or aggression, and at times, these particular decisions resulted in more trouble for her and her friends. 
 Her saving grace is that at times, she could be quite humorous. She has a particularly sharp-tongued, witty form of response, especially when she has her guard up. She's also fiercely loyal and this extends to people beyond her brother as the novel progresses. 
 Jack is the first friendly male we meet after Lugh's capture, and this takes place a considerable time after Saba's initial decision to leave Silverlake. He's also presented as a mystery which needs to be solved, so he feels important, yet remains distant while some of the plot progresses. At about a third of the way through, we finally have our first conversation with him, but Saba is on edge, with her defences up, so we don't get to meet all of him at once. However, for me, I found that was enough to make me want to see more of him. He met Saba's sturdy walls with a wry humour - the same that Saba is capable of and often returned in kind. 
 I did like Jack. True to his name, he does have a rather 'Jack-the-lad' attitude about him which was infectious. He does things with an optimism and a smile which contrasts greatly with the bleak existence of the wasteland. His cheek and sarcasm meets Saba's stony attitude perfectly and is probably the only thing that effectively brings her back to ground level. I felt the pace and tone picked up once Jack had more of a presence. 
 At first, I was drawn in by the premise of the narrative. What kept me was the presentation of the story. This is a first person narrative written by Saba. As a result, the spelling and syntax reflects Saba's voice and tone. I love books that do this. While at first it was a bit jarring as I tripped over the deliberate misspellings, it became the one thing that absorbed me into the world Young was depicting. Here's a bit of an example: 
 "Lugh's bin sayin it fer a while now. Pa's gitten worse. Mind you, he ain't bin right fer a long time." 
 It sounds so much more like a conversation between you and Saba that you as the reader are able to connect with her on some form of level, despite the way she hides herself away and keeps herself to herself. She doesn't open up to any of the characters, but this style of writing shows that she will open herself up to the reader. You can start to understand why she is so guarded, even if you might wish she wasn't. 
 Last Thoughts 
 This is a good start to the trilogy and was enough to allow me to invest something into each character. I have left wanting to revisit this world and catch up with its inhabitants. I hope that we get to see a softer side to Saba and have the opportunity to see the other characters receive some further development. The novel ended quite openly, so I have no idea what to expect from the next instalment. I am very much looking forward to it. 
 Reading Recommendation: Read it! 
 TL;DR 
 Think Mad Max with a young, female protagonists and without all of the cars. Horsemen capture Saba's brother and she'll do anything to get him back. Cue a very angry journey to get him back.
Enjoyable all around, and I can see why it ended as it did, but I would have preferred that Donovan play a larger role.

<<Overview>> 
 Flawlessly paced. Volumes 1 and 2 seemed to pass in the blink of an eye, and while Volume 3 was still a fast read, it felt like a complete arc. It also, unsurprisingly, left me desperate for more. 
 Take your copy of Volume 3. Flip it over. Take a minute to just appreciate how effing hot Alana and Marko are. 
 ALL THE FEELS. All of them were felt in this volume, from laughter, to suspense, to happy tears, to heartbreak. 
 <<Plot>> 
 The story does a tiny rewind and backs up to a few days before Volume 2 ended. A couple of new characters are introduced, and our happy family arrives on the planet Quietus. After Alana proves herself to totally be the most badass mom ever (wielding a mace against a bone monster, all with baby Hazel safely in her arms), we get a very unimpressive introduction to D. Oswald Heist. As the story says, "But no one makes worse first impressions than writers." They all join him in his lovely lighthouse home, and all seems well until the inevitable arrives, something we know is coming: Prince Robot IV. 
 The Will, Gwendolyn, and Slave Girl are stranded on a lush, exotic planet. While waiting to get the ship fixed, The Will renames Slave Girl as Sophie, and also starts hallucinating about The Stalk in a very Battlestar Galatica way (was I the only one picturing Gaius and Six while he was having a conversation with both Gwendolyn and his hallucination?). After being wishy-washy about wanting to continue his pursuit of Alana, Marko, Hazel, and IV, a rather momentous event occurs that causes Gwendolyn to seek out Marko's help, rather than his head on a stick. 
 Also, the page solely between Sophie and Lying Cat. It will simultaneously melt and break your heart all at once. I had chin wibbles. You'll know it when you see it. 
 We also meet two new characters, Upshet and Doff, a couple of journalists (and the first gay couple we're officially introduced to as characters) in pursuit of the story of a lifetime. The story of Alana and Marko and their darling lovechild is one neither side wants to let out, and it makes them some serious enemies straight out of the gate. Even with their tongues tired, I doubt this will be the last we see of this duo. 
 Oh, and all the Robots are assholes. Not a surprise. 
 Annnd...spoilers! 
  Sophie stabbing The Will! Nooo! I really don't want The Will's character out of play for long, especially with Gwendolyn's admission to love at the end. 
 Gale was totally lying about Alana, right? Right?! He just said that to throw Upshet and Doff off the scent. He wouldn't just spill such a big secret to two nobody reporters, right...? 
 Heist's death was awful. I don't think I've ever had such a reaction to a character death in a graphic novel before. His bond with Klara, and the family, and just...ugh. They already took Barr from us, why did they have to take Heist too?  
 <<Cast>> 
 Some of this could get spoiler-y, so read at your own caution. 
 D. Oswald Heist makes yet another fabulous character introduction: totally drunk, wearing nothing bug a robe and slippers, and promptly puking all over baby Hazel. But, of course, that's only our first impression. Heist is a very kind, generous, and intelligent man. He immediately bonds with Klara over the loss of their loved ones. (The sentiment they share over the pain of losing your partner being worse than losing your child. Ungh. It killed me.) He takes to the family, and becomes an unbeatable schemer with Klara in planting ideas into the happy couple's head about their future. I was so very sad that we don't have him in the story anymore. 
 I do love Klara, as well. She's so snarky, but it's obvious she cares about her granddaughter. While she obviously struggles with Alana's race moreso than her late husband, you can tell she's coming around, and that she plans to protect and help her family, no matter what. She can be abrasive, but she has the young family's best interests at heart. I love having her acidity around to tamper down the sweetness of Alana and Marko. There's mutual respect building between Alana and Klara as well, like how Alana wouldn't throw an arm-wrestling match to her new mother-in-law just because she's wounded and grieving. They're beginning to respect one another's strength. 
 Gwendolyn is developed more in this volume as well, and I'm impressed. She catches on to the hallucinogenic food like a lightning bolt. She also proves that she's not just all about revenge when she seeks out Marko's help for The Will, putting aside her need for revenge in the face of losing someone she only recently admits to loving. 
 Alana's little booknerd moments nearly killed me. When she actually said "bookgasm" out loud, and freaked out over spoilers to Heist's next book. Gah! Not to mention, we learn how Hazel got her name. The couple named her after the librarian that first introduced Alana to Heist's books. How freaking adorable is that? 
 Upshet and Doff don't get too much actual character development this time around, besides being journalists and being a couple on a planet that severely frowns on homosexuality. I hope to see more of them because, yay diversity! 
 We also get a glimpse at The Will's sister, The Brand. The Brand has a ridiculously animal companion, an evil Saint Bernard that can shoot darts out of its nose. I kind of want one. Also, it was lovely to see some vulnerability and emotion when it comes to the bounty hunters. The scene with her in the hospital with The Will, calling him by his real name and getting teary? Just wonderful. How sweet is it that The Will named Slave Girl after his sister, too? 
 <<Art>> 
 I'm slowly becoming convinced that there is no comic book artist that can compare to Fiona Staples. From neon sky sharks, to naked unicorn ladies, she tackles it all and it makes perfect sense. She can convey a lot of emotion in her characters' faces, her world-building is jaw-dropping, and her color palette just makes you want to sink right into the pages. Everything is lush and vibrant and unique. 
 I also don't know if this is just the benefit of having a female artist that doesn't have to follow any rules (because Saga obviously has none), but the diversity of body imagery is refreshing. I know there are a lot of issues in the comic world with how women are portrayed, and I feel Saga really tackles that. Alana's stepmother, Even, is short and pear-shaped, with an obvious tummy-pooch, even though she's young. Gwendolyn is tall and lanky, athletic with very little curve.  /// 
 Sky has lead a sheltered life. Adopted as a toddler, she's survived until now with no television, telephones or internet. Now, it's her senior year and she's managed to convince her mother to attend public school. Being home schooled her entire life hasn't hindered Sky's extracurricular activities though, and with some help from her neighbor and best friend, Sky's already got a reputation. Making it worse, her friend is doing a semester abroad, leaving Sky to fend for herself. 
 Dean's been gone for last year. If you believe the rumors, that year was spent in juvie. Now he's back in town and on a collision course with Sky. The first time they meet is an intense experience, leaving Sky feeling shaken. Use to feeling numb, the emotions Dean makes Sky feel after only a few moments rattle her. Sky knows she should stay away from him, but he's not going to make it easier. 
 As Sky and Dean spend time together, she realizes that he might not be who he claims. He's hiding something, something big. When the truth is revealed, Sky will learn that there are worse things than feeling numb. Some things are just hopeless. 
 /// 
 [ Spoilered Review ] 
 While I really liked this story, it wasn't without a few weaknesses. 
 Hoover gives us another emotional, intense read and a great cast of characters with Hopeless. I love her character building. She's able to create unique personalities, each with distinctive voices. She's also so good at developing characters through the challenges they face. The book also held a good pace through most of the story. It had the right mix of romance, drama and mystery. The flashback chapters were well placed, giving enough enough away to help the reader try to piece it together and think they've got it all figure out - which makes the true "holy shit" moment far more unexpected and shocking. 
 My issue with the pace of the book comes with the scene involving Sky's confrontation with her father. It was too short, too undeveloped and not that well placed within the story. It caused the rest of the story to really drag. They argue, a gun is drawn and he blows his damn head off. And then...that's it. Sky and Holder drive off to the hotel and that's the end of it. No consequences, nothing more is really said about the incident afterwards. To me, that should have been one of the the big moments of the book. Sky confronts the catalyst for her entire life, the reason for her broken memories and stolen life and the entire thing was so...lackluster and blah. The rest of the book was still good, but by then it just felt like a lot of fluff. 
 All in all, this is another solid addition to my bookshelf. Hoover has become an "I will read anything you write" author for me, and this book is no exception. 4/5 stars for this one.

 Only Mira Grant could write a series about tapeworm horror, and make it compelling, intelligent, well thought out and absolutely terrifying. 
 The Parasitology series explores a world dominated by science, where people rely on tapeworm implants for perfect health and longevity. While Parasite explored how this technology was invented and how it was adopted across the globe, Symbiont explores the detrimental and disastrous effects of the implant, as people using implants become cold, empty shells - or zombies. 
 As an avid zombie fan, I've heard about diseases, bites and airbourne viruses causing the affliction, but this is the first time tapeworms have become the primary cause of death. It's sickly fascinating, gruesome and unimaginable - but somehow, with the justification of science, it becomes believable in this dark and chilling world. 
 I won't provide any spoilers for Parasite, but Symbiont was as chilling and addictive as the first. As if the tapeworms and zombies weren't enough, Sal experiences many dark and sinister situations totally out of her control. From being strapped down by a military organisation, to being operated on by scientists, to being held captive against her will by a sick man, I experienced complete and utter horror at some of these situations and the immoral and evil behaviour of people once the world goes mad. 
 Sal's genuine, intelligent and inquisitive nature makes her a survivor, and I was proud of her leadership, strength and resolve no matter how dangerous the situation. While the events of Parasite left her reeling and unsure of herself, she really grows in confidence by the end of the book. Symbiont made me love Nathan more, in all of his geeky, scientific glory and his loyalty and love for Sal. 
 We are introduced to some fantastic new characters, from Ronnie, the tapeworm assassin who is stuck in a man's body, to Fishy, a man in denial who believes he's stuck in a video game. 
 There are a few problems with plot continuity however, as without the kidnapping and saving, not much actually happened in the book. At over 600 pages, you'd expect more to happen outside of repeating the events of the previous book and having our character being thrust in a whole range of situations. 
 Symbiont is not just a book about tapeworms, or zombies, or even science. It explores the scary effects of a world relying on an untested technology, opposing views of different scientists and organisations, and the blurred lines between human, scientific subject and tapeworm. From tapeworms burrowing into our skulls, to scientists on the ruthless quest for knowledge to evil profiteering companies, there are so many terrifying situations in this book. 
 It also leaves us with the chilling notion - if we discovered an incredibly risky cure to all diseases, would we use it?

I'm not sure if this is due to a lack of rigorous outlining and planning (he often states that books just "write themselves", indicating the lack of a clear conception of the story's resolution ahead of time), or due to uninspired ideas, but he has something of a reputation in this regard. 
 Here's another story in which the gripping plot, multi-dimensional characters, and essential drama that kept me up until the wee hours of 4 consecutive mornings were cheapened by a hokey and trite conclusion.  I mean, would it kill him to write a book in which the boogieman wasn't from another world, galaxy, or dimension? The thing is - I believe he could pull it off easily. With no more than 20 pages of edits, this could've been a completely different book; one that makes a profound statement about political posturing, greed, despotic power, and the actions of people placed under a great deal of stress. The book still does that, I think, but it will certainly appeal to a much narrower audience as written . 
 So why the 5 stars? Because even though the conclusion was disappointing, it was one hell of a ride. I've already begun the process of constructing a mental wall around those 20-ish pages that so disappointed me. Those pages never existed. I've convinced myself that I can't remember the ending, or maybe that the ending didn't really matter. The most important part of this novel (and most of Stephen King's other novels) are the characters. Under the Dome is one of the most riveting portrayals of groupthink I've ever read. It's almost as if the story is a biography of Chester's Mill (the town cut off by the dome), an apparently healthy character who suddenly develops a virulent cancer, with a few malignant cells spreading like wildfire and leaving the body a wasted ruin within a matter of days. 
 Worth the read for anyone who loves character-driven novels, small-town politics, or supernatural stories (although the latter isn't necessary if you can quarantine a few pages in your brain).

One thing I did not realize when I started this book was that it contained a map of Chester's Mill. I completely skipped over it, and let me tell you, it would have helped a lot. 
 But anyway. This was an engaging, fast read (despite its size - I got through it in less than a week), entertaining and gruesome and just a little bit crazy. In other words, business as usual, at least for a Stephen King novel. 
 I'm not really one for writing out full reviews, so I'm just going to leave a couple of observations/questions here: 
 1) Can a dome really be a dome if it adheres to the boundaries of a sock-shaped town? 
 2) Does Stephen King have some weird, unnecessary axe to grind against feminists? I remember he made some comment about them in Bag of Bones (which was pretty rich, considering the forty-something male protagonist didn't see anything wrong with lusting after a nineteen-year-old woman and sexualizing her three-year-old daughter, but I digress), and the same is true in Under the Dome. I'll include the full quote here, because it really is cringeworthy: 
 "When Howie got you all to the station, DeLesseps told Howie that you raped Angie McCain. Isn't that how it went?" 
 "That was his first story. Then he said maybe it wasn't quite rape, but when she got scared and told me to stop, I wouldn't. That would make it rape in the second degree, I guess." 
 She smiled briefly. "Don't let any feminists hear you say there are degrees of rape." 
 "I guess I better not." 
 This exchange between Dale Barbara, one of the novel's protagonists, and Brenda Perkins, another one of the "good guys," is seriously mindblowing. Newsflash, Stephen King: if you're having sex with a girl and she tells you to stop, and you keep going, that's still rape! No "degrees" about it! What kind of Whoopi Goldberg "it's not rape rape" bullshit? 
 And before you stop me and say, "Wait a minute, anolinde, this is all fiction, just because Stephen King's characters say something doesn't mean he endorses their viewpoints," well, that's all fine and dandy, but the fact of the matter is that these comments are coming from two people whom the audience is expected to sympathize with and root for. They're among the few in Chester's Mill smart enough to get the town out of this mess, and they've been "right" all along. So if Stephen King doesn't agree with their comments, he's nevertheless implicitly endorsing them, and certainly no one in the novel - no one the reader will side with, anyway - offers a different opinion. 
 But those feminists, man. 
 3) I'm not sure I buy that everything unraveled so quickly (Chester's Mill has pretty much gone to shit by the second or third day). I suppose it could have, especially considering the powder keg of issues and incompetent, power-hungry officials, but it all seemed to happen very fast. 
 4) The whole leatherhead thing was very weird. I suppose it's par for the course with Stephen King novels, but the explanation for the Dome's existence left me with more questions than answers. If we're drawing parallels between the leatherheads and children who set ants on fire with magnifying glasses, why hasn't the Dome happened before to other towns? And if they're an entirely different species, why are their living spaces and social dynamics so similar to those of humans?  
 5) On a somewhat related note, I'm probably not going to watch the TV series, because I imagine it would be a little too grim and depressing for my tastes... but the guy they picked to play Dale Barbara is damn fine.

Trigger Warning: Sexual assault. Details: Long term sexual assault of a minor by a person in authority. Psuedo-incest (parental figure). Neglectful parenting. Sexualisation of a young girl by a parent.  
 Synopsis: Mandy is pregnant, and wants to find a nice family who can give her child the chances she never had. Jill's Dad recently died, and in the face of mortality and not having done enough, her Mom wants to adopt a baby (and can't wait for normal channels). Jill is just trying to deal with her batshit Mom who thinks adopting a baby will replace the giant hole where her Dad should be. 
 I loved the dual point of view of this book. 
 For Jill McSweeney, this is a reimagining of someone who has already done their coming of age story. She was sorted, she knew who she was, and then life threw her a loop when her Dad died. But her story is about making her more than herself, rocking her own boat, pushing her back into a world with other people. 
 For Mandy Kalinowski, this is a coming of age, a claiming of agency at the very beginning when she has never had that in her hands before. And it's a regression to childhood as well. She was forced to grow up and never had a childhood, a carer, *fun*. She can't have a coming of age story, because she isn't going from childhood to adulthood, she's going from some fucked up psuedo-adulthood to the first time she's allowed to think for herself. 
 The contrast is fucking awesome. 
 I loved Jill's mother. She is badass, and demanding, and mid-life-crisis-ing. But, damn it, she knows her own mind and she's not going to stop herself because of what other people (including her daughter) think of her. 
 I loved how extraordinarily uncomfortable reading Mandy's point of view made me. She is young, and a liar, and distinct, and appears so unrelentingly shallow. I hated being caught in her point of view for the first part, because everything she did, or said, or remembered made me hate everything and want to run away. She's caught in a world in her own head where everything is echoes of things her mother said, things she thinks are right, things she thinks are important. 
 But this is a class narrative. Mandy is so uncomfortably trapped in the lower social class she comes from, with no chances in life, and it is fully and tangibly and horrifically reflected in her narrative voice. So many contemporary YA protagonists are middle class aspiring authors (Jill works in a not so subtly disguised Borders), and she only knows gossip mags, and thinks her pretty blondeness is all she will ever have. That is what she knows. She thinks she has to be on permanent seduction mode (from the time of her first period, when her mother proclaimed her a woman, an object for men). She would protect herself, but doesn't know how. She has never had anyone protect her. (Forgive me if that sounds classist myself, I don't intend it to. Her mother reads as a terrifying amalgam of Jerry Springer participants. It's a commentary on class defining your life chances and choices.) 
 I love Mandy. I want to hug her, and hold her, and make sure everything is okay, and slowly try to pull her to a new understanding of her own worth as a human. 
 I love that there is no blushing virgin-falling-in-love trope, even if Mandy is jaded and innocent simultaneously. Jill has sex, and she's had sex before, and she'll have sex again, and her relationships (platonically and romantically) are in trouble in adult ways, not young, first relationship drama ways. 
 I love the delicacy of how sexual abuse is dealt with. I love how Mandy is still indoctrinated enough to believe in love (sort of), and uses that as a protective mechanism against her own memories. 
 I love the multi-racial couples. (Yay, diversity! Numerous examples of different coloured diversity! Racism acknowledged as a force in the world, but fuck it, we're diverse.) 
 I love the families of choice. I love the relationships which weird people who usually wouldn't get scenes together have, and explore, and develop. 
 This is an excellent novel. It wasn't perfect, but what I loved about it I loved deeply. It shook me up, and made me feel sick, and I grew to love a character I couldn't stand when she walked in.

 Ready Player One is a futuristic novel for 80's fans or video game geeks. Luckily I fall somewhere between the two, but I think the novel works best for people where 70% of the references weren't lost on them. At least I recognized the Monty Python and some of the music. 
 The main character, Wade, is an 18 year old geek who is one of the million people known as "gunters" or, "egg-hunters". OASIS is a virtual reality that is reality for many people in the world, and before the creator died, he left behind an Easter Egg in the game that would allow his accumulated wealth/his ownership of OASIS to be bequeathed upon whoever found it first. 
 Wade, or, by his IGN, Parzival, is the one who finds the first of three keys that leads to the Easter Egg itself. He has to deal with rocky relationships between him and his closest gunter friends, opposition from a powerful corporation force that will literally stop at nothing to be the ones to gain ownership of OASIS, blurring the lines between virtual reality and the real world (harming them IRL and online, you know the drill), and a real world that's nearly dystopian in its bleakness. 
 Wait a second, nix the last one, I guess, because it isn't developed nearly enough. Seriously. You have a world where half the population spends their time fully immersed in a virtual reality that's almost entirely like real life, and the rest of the world has apparently been plunged into constant famine and warfare, and it never matters? 
 The main character, Wade, has some serious author self-insertion issues going on. He borders on gary stu status. But never quite gets there, I guess. He's close enough to the line that it's noticeable and irritating. 
 Aech was a redeeming factor. Without spoiling anything, their character is intriguing and keeps things moving. 
 Eh.

Ender's Game is one of those books that everyone just assumes you read in school as assigned reading, then they look shocked when they discover you hadn't. Well, now I have. 
 It's an interesting science-fiction book, and definitely would be classified as "young adult" now. The story--in case you also are late to the party--is about Ender Wiggen, a genius-level boy who is selected by mysterious government men to join the Battle School. These men are entrusted with the care of many such excellent children, with the goal of training them to be perfect soldiers, and, in Ender's case, the perfect commander, in the human fight against the alien buggers. Because of this, Ender is subjected to trial after trial, both interpersonal as well as intellectual. He is isolated and suffers much. Meanwhile, back at home, his also-genius and somewhat sociopathic siblings Valentine and Peter concoct their own schemes to meddle in Earth politics and gain power...even as children. 
 The book really shines in the zero-G/null gravity tactical battles, which, according to the preface written by author Orson Scott Card, was what started the whole thing anyway. Card tackles the challenges of combat--distance and hand-to-hand--in three dimensions, adding challenges we just won't face on Earth (hopefully). It's easy to see why directors thought this would make a great movie; these scenes are vivid and enthralling. 
 Otherwise, I found the story a little far-fetched. Ender a super-duper genius at just 6? He certainly doesn't have interactions like a 6-year-old. I'll accede that possibly he could be really smart and particularly verbal and accept the language as it is, but even super-geniuses need a certain level of human companionship. I also don't know that I ever fully bought into the validity of the scheme of isolation to produce leadership, that having no friends was explicitly what was going to make Ender a good leader. Which is one of the main conceits of the book... 
 Card notes in his preface that, when the book was first published, he received angry letters from parents who claimed no gifted child would talk like that. I'm not sure I see anything that seems totally out of the realm of possibility...not just for gifted children, but for any children. Kids can be sadistic bastards, yo. (And I think we as a culture may have gotten over that squeamishness some, at least in fiction, with Harry Potter and Katniss Everdeen, among many others, being highly cogent.) 
 I love the space stuff, but don't particularly love the overall message and themes of this book. Perhaps I'm too old to really appreciate the tortured-youth of it; the adults just seem like unforgivable assholes to me. 
 The ending--the final ending, after the buggers have been defeated--felt so horribly tacked-on and unformed that it really took a lot away from the book for me. It felt like Card desperately wanted a happy ending for this character he unduly tortured but didn't know how to get there, so slapped together 20 pages of falderal so he can write sequels. While I'm glad I finally read this book, I don't think I'll be pursuing the others. 
 Card's highly controversial/offensive personal views--he is an active Mormon and has been outspoken about his disgust toward homosexuality, and has been a generous donor to anti-gay marriage folks--is interesting. I bought this book second-hand because I don't support his views personally and therefore didn't want extra money going to him, and perhaps that made it top-of-mind for me...but for all that he was anti-homosexuality, his book could very easily be read as including it in a positive way. It's something the reader would have to bring to the book, so to speak, but there's an awful lot of male nudity (I wish I'd kept tabs on how often the word "naked" was used!) and there's a fight scene in a shower featuring highly lathered and soapy naked teenage boys. There are barely two female characters in the whole book; it's not a huge leap. Worth thinking about, anyway. 
 (Related: I found it interesting/odd that religion is apparently gone from this Earth at the beginning of the book--banned, it seems--except that Jews are held in high regard, and by the end Ender has inadvertently created a religion? That seemed inconsistent.)

The Court of the Owls *should* have more impact on me than they do - why is that? They're menacing, they know all about Bruce/Batman, they're nigh-unstoppable, they're sociopathic. They just keep coming, and have untold numbers. 
 Wait, y'know what? They're just another version of The Hand, and we all know from Daredevil and Wolverine tales that they're always beatable when there's so many of them (as opposed to the lone unstoppable sociopath who's oddly harder to beat). 
 Mr. Freeze's story is more interesting - an Origin story, sure - but also has a few notes of tragedy and humanity that the Court of Owls lack. Impregnable villains are always less interesting than the ones to whom, through some small crack, we can relate. 
 Thomas is a classic Silver Age/Batman '66 villain - monologues the shit out of Batman while he holds him in a supposedly perfectly victimised position, only to (despite the constant blather) fall victim to his own hubris. Good god is that an exercise in surviving death-by-boredom. Far better is Alfred's father's tale, weaving in some interesting background details and trussing together the fragments of the past Snyder stories. 
 The "Ghost in the Machine" story was great - a departure from surrounding Bruce with claustrophobic attention, giving us a look at a potential new supporting character who will be awesome if Snyder lets her be herself. Cloonan's art was good too. 
 Which brings us to the clown car of artists this book contains. What the hell, DC? Is this deliberate sabotage on your flagship title? Or a way to take a small risk on a book no one will stop buying, to showcase a revolving door of new artists? The quality is good, and I would probably enjoy each in turn, but c'mon - you know that the current fashion is to keep one creative team together to establish a following, a style, a "run". This has to be killing Snyder to adapt to all these other creators. Did he poss someone off?

My girls all adore Sarah Dessen, but this was the first of her books I've actually read. It was sweet! And made me want pizza. 
 One of the reasons I've never been terribly motivated to read Dessen's books is because they seem, to me, to be pretty straightforward romances. Now don't get me wrong: romance, swoon, whatever, is a HUGE part of YA fiction. It's incredibly rare to come across a young adult novel that doesn't *somehow* involve a love story (I secretly love it when it happens though. It's like finding a unicorn!). But I just prefer my stories to have more going on than just a relationship. I've written about my distaste for genre romance before: it's what sank the All Souls trilogy for me (ironically NOT a YA series). I can't handle when whatever semblance of a plot there is screams to a dead halt in its tracks while we sit around and discuss our pwecious feewings. Barf. I'm also a much bigger fantasy/sci fi nerd than I realized, so something that's contemporary realistic fiction has to be *really* intriguing for me to sit up and take notice. And sadly, realistic YA usually turns into romance (or death, which is depressing for the obvious reasons). 
 This is all to say that I ended up being pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this book. Yes, there is romance and feewings, but there's also *there* there. Protagonist Sydney is trying to cope with being the "good" daughter after her brother drives drunk and puts another boy in a wheelchair. She decides to switch schools for a fresh start and falls into the orbit of the Chatham family, who own a local pizzeria. She and Layla become besties almost immediately, and of course the instant Sydney lays eyes on Layla's brother Mac, it's clear that he will be the love interest. To be fair, even though it's completely predictable, it's dealt with in a realistic way, and I have to admit I did find myself rooting for those two kids to get together! And I loved their bonding over her pizza-whispering skills. Predictable does not have to mean boring -- it's like comfort food. 
 Speaking of which, so much food in this book. The Chathams own the aforementioned pizzeria, and Layla is obsessed with French fries. She has a rating scale and a special spice blend for ketchup, and clearly some kind of crazy metabolism to process it all, considering she and Sydney eat several slices of pizza daily, plus fries at lunch. And it's not like Dessen's just ignoring the concept of weight gain, because there's this whole thing about how Mac lost tons of weight and is super disciplined. It's just strange. Also, Layla's "preparations" for eating fries bothered me: the best fries are hot fries, no matter where you got them. When you spend a full five minutes "preparing" different ketchup piles, you end up with the worst kind of fries: cold ones. Even so, still made me crave French fries (and now I'm trying to figure out which place in Springfield would have the best ones...I'm weirdly partial to Obed's). 
 Anyway, this is cute, but it does have substance. A few of the Stanford family subplots went on too long and thus had to be resolved too quickly; like the whole thing with creepy Ames. I realize the whole point is that the mom has a blind spot where the son is concerned, so she kind of refuses to see Ames for the obvious sexual predator he is, but it all turns on a dime. One minute he's living there, the next minute they're kicking him out and they're immune to his charms. And the hyper-control freak mom was just infuriating. I know people like her exist, but that doesn't mean I want to read about them. I guess she does mellow a bit in the end, but again, it happens so quickly it's almost not satisfying.  
 I'm glad I gave Dessen a chance, and while I'm not rushing out to read more of her stuff right away, it's nice to know I can be wrong about romances sometimes.

First off, let's talk about how much I love Radu.

 Then we get this beautiful family dynamic between Radu, Nazira, and Fatima. They are all just such amazing people and they deserve every good thing to happen to them. Nazira was such a queen in this book and it made my life. I was so excited that Kiersten gave her a bigger role in this book. I hope in the next book we get to see even more of Fatima as well because we (and by we I mean Radu and me, of course) kept getting hints and I was like I love this cinnamon roll so much and I need to know her entire backstory right now so I can keep her safe and protected forevermore. 
 That's one thing that I think Kiersten did super well in this sequel-- she brought back minor characters from And I Darken and gave them pivotal roles. It was just so well done and I love when authors do that because I feel like it shows that they really respect their readers to care about details and continuity instead of just always creating new characters. *pats Kiersten White on the back* I just reread And I Darken a week ago and Kiersten brought back a character that must have been mentioned in literally one sentence in the first book and now he is a new fave of mine. 
 I also really loved how the back and forth between Radu's and Lada's plotlines were so consistent. Their two storylines were pretty separate for the entire book and usually I don't like that because I like when they merge at some point. But I think this book did a really good job of it as I was equally interested in both storylines, so I never wanted to stop reading. 
 Kiersten is really a master of making the worst thing that could possibly happen to a character happen and forcing that character to deal with the repercussions. I was so frustrated throughout the entire book because I couldn't give the characters advice. Especially knowing historically about the fall of Constantinople, which for some reason was one of the most emphasized events in all of my two years of high school global/world history classes. I knew what was going to happen and the dramatic irony was killing me. I feel like readers who know nothing of Ottoman history will still really enjoy the book regardless, but having a little background info made me feel really invested in the story, especially on top of my deep investment with Radu's wellbeing. 
 Okay so I don't know how I got this far into the review without talking about Lada?? I love her a lot, even though her sections in this book didn't feel *quite* as relevant or urgent as they did in the last book (she sort of fell a little bit on the backburner for me behind everything that was going on with Radu, but I still loved reading about her). Reading about Lada reminds me of the way I felt when I first read about Celaena Sardothein in Throne of Glass. She's just so cool and badass. I love how morally gray she is, but at the same time she was like so empowering. I especially loved the contrast between Radu and Lada's chapters when Radu would be like we can't let this one random person die because it's not right, and then immediately after we'll see Lada stabbing like an entire army. 
 All in all, I was so satisfied with this sequel. I found reading about the characters now that they are older was much more interesting for me. I can't wait for the next book when all the character's will somehow inevitably be brought together. (*whispers* I hope Radu realizes he is way too good for Mehmed and joins Lada and they take over the world... that's a totally acceptable creative freedom from history right??) I loooved the letters in the last two chapters of the book even though they sort of made me want to cry. It was such a strong ending and it made me so excited for the concluding novel!

 Gah, this book. It was probably 4.5 stars for me going into the ending. There were so many things to appreciate about it, and just a few things that bothered me*. On a stylistic level, I thought King's writing was strong - emotional and evocative. Thematically and politically, King's portrayal of the start of modern anthropological ethnography was nuanced and balanced - Nell Stone (aka Margaret Mead) and her compatriots were among the first to think about bias and objectivity and global white supremacy, and they were all part of changing anthropology into what we see today. I thought King's portrayal of the native peoples' Stone lived with and studied in New Guinea was equally nuanced. She shows that what we know of this people has come through the lens of white anthropologists, who themselves knew that they weren't getting or understanding everything. She wrote the indigenous characters as people, which ideally wouldn't be a positive thing to note. (Ideally it would just be a thing that everybody does, but instead here I am, thankful that she treated human beings like human beings.) King engages with the complicated harm that white people brought to the rest of the world, especially in the return of an indigenous man who had gone off to work in a mine and came back changed. 
 That's the good stuff out of the way. My niggling negatives pre-ending included a discomfort with how unclear it is what is Margaret Mead & compatriots and what is fictionalized. King changes enough, including making Stone more passive than Mead and her husband both emotionally and physically abusive when afaik there isn't evidence of that, that I would have appreciated more notes in the back, separating truth from fiction. I also felt uncomfortable with King's POV choices - why does Bankson get this close, personal 1st person perspective, while Stone gets either a limited-3rd or diary entries? Ultimately, King's POVs show her focus: this is really Bankson's story, about how Stone saved him and his career, and it seems insulting to me, to take one of the most famous & fascinating women in history and write a book about how she changed one man's life. Judging harshly, I'm going to say that King turned Mead into a Manic Pixie Dream Girl, with a little less manic pixie, but plenty of "amazing, crazy, unique girl comes into a man's life and inspire/save him." Ughughgughgughg. 
 And worse than that, worse than *that*, and here's where we get to my deep anger at the ending, King kills her. It's not enough for Stone to save Bankson's life/career, she has to DIE. If I was insulted by the former, I am enraged by the latter. Bankson goes on to become a famous and accomplished anthropologist and Nell Stone dies. Bankson is heartbroken and Nell Stone has been, imo, fridged.  
 I will say that it is rare for me to downgrade a book more than half a star based on its ending (I only had one last year - Meg Wolitzer's Belzhar), so for me to go down 2 full stars is a big deal. I rounded up to 3 stars out of respect for the nuance and care King showed during most of the book. 
 *Thank you, Mia, for helping me to, rather than fall into to a rage cycle, think through my post-reading anger and to acknowledge all of the things I appreciated about the book.

Almost 2.5 Stars 
 Set in the early 1990's, this book is strongly reminiscent of The Wonder Years--but lacking the more hopeful undertones and genuine nostalgia. 
 The epistolary narrative style carries the unfortunate problem of limited or non-existent setting and physical descriptions, as readers are relegated to the pinhole perspective of the main character and sole POV, Charlie. (If not for the existence of the movie adaptation, this reader would have little to go on by way of imagery.) As Charlie puts his thoughts into letter form, it quickly becomes apparent that he is neurologically atypical. Everything about his characterization screams Asperger's autism, but as the story takes place a decade before the spectrum became more widely recognized, readers are left to wonder over the actual cause of his social impairments. 
 Charlie is a generally sympathetic character who sometimes borders on pitiable. He's a 15-year-old supposedly "gifted" freshman who has great difficulty connecting with people. (I say 'supposedly' because his written voice sounds more like a semi-organized 11 or 12-year-old, at about the same maturity level.) Charlie happens to fall into the good graces of a pack of party-crowd hipster seniors, who take him under their tattered and broadminded wings. Each of them is a questionably functional mess in their own way, and they are happy to draw the painfully naive Charlie into their version of reality. 
 Ultimately this isn't just an "issues" book, it is the kitchen sink of issues books. 
 I can't recall seeing so many traumas, negative coping mechanisms, and destructive behavioral patterns crammed (somewhat casually) into one plotline. Suicide, rape, domestic abuse, child molestation, depression, abortion, bullying, vehicular death, crippling anxiety, substance abuse, repressed memories, psychological breaks, anonymous gay sex, and ...*drumroll* ... incest. >.> I'm pretty sure all it lacked was a terminal ailment. 
 The problem isn't so much the content itself as the handling. That is to say, none of these issues end up feeling satisfactorily addressed or explored to any meaningful extent. 
 As far as the writing itself goes, the characterization falls a bit flat--especially in the adults. (Although one could argue this is in part due to Charlie's perceptions, as he's something of an unreliable narrator.) The pacing is sedate, the dialogue is unmemorable, and there isn't much by way of an evident goal/endgame to build anticipation. 
 Two vaguely redeeming qualities include the fact that Charlie is actually receiving some psychological help... And toward the end, he is finally called out for simply being present to watch one of his "friends" self-destruct while passively failing to intervene in any way. But on the whole, it's a sizable time investment that yields too little substance for this reader to be able to recommend it in good conscience.

I am far too old to be in the target audience for this series, so the moral quandary that made up the bulk of this book mostly just frustrated me. It's a bit like a family sitcom where the kids are smarter than the adults. Certainly one could argue that the adults have become calcified in their ways of thinking and that in these new situations, new (young) points of view are necessary to adapt and survive. 
 I'm still not certain what The Weapon was, or what the leaders thought they would gain by using it on a mixed crowd of people, but I liked that it set the fire that allowed both Doon and Lina to be the heroes. I kept thinking, the way that the author kept describing the weather, that a tornado was going to appear and flatten the town, requiring everyone to work together to survive. The fire was the better choice, because it made the leaders culpable, it remained a manageable sort of disaster, and no one lost a trailer.  
 I would definitely recommend this series to kids -- it is gentle post-apocalyptic fiction, with a little bit of danger; and puzzling out the historical artifacts from our own times is a little bonus.

I feel somewhat sorry for the dragons in this. They spent the entirety of the Liveship Trader's trilogy trying to find a place to evolve out of their basic serpent form, and when they do find it most of them die in the process. They're too mutated and twisted to be able to develop into dragons. Only fourteen remain by the end and even those are stunted and unusual, that much so that the dragon Tintaglia abandons them for a richer prospect, mating with the ancient dragon Icefyre in Fool's Fate. So they're on their own. 
 Nobody wants them 
 These new dragons are a nuisance. The Rain Wild folk want them gone because they are a blight on their recourses; they want them gone because they are growing increasingly dangerous and are wanting more and more food as they get even bigger. In addition, some mutated teenagers amongst their own people are a so called embarrassment to civilisation. So, ever so pragmatically, the rulers decide to pair up one of these weird kids with a dragon and send them off on their own looking for an ancient city. Sounds like a great move? They lose two problems, but don't really consider the consequence of possible success. 
 Thymara has been hated all her life for her lizard features; thus, when a chance like this comes up she jumps at it, and who can blame her. Not many people get to interact with dragons albeit stunted ones. Her dragon, however, is haughty and superior; she distains all those she perceives as beneath her. So Tymara has a rather interesting task on her hands, which leads to some difficult and amusing situations. She has to deal with a dragon who thinks herself a god of the sky when in reality she is half grown and misshapen, and is struggling to accept the realities of who she is. It seems to me these two are perfectly suited to each other. 
 They are driven by ancient memories 
 I love the complexities of the dragons here. They remember all the lives of their ancestors, and they consume the bodies of dead dragons to gain more memories. This way the dragons are wise and experienced without having to do anything to get such gifts. This means that these dragons, though young, know exactly how to salvage their situation and grow into their destinies as rulers of the sky. They are instinctively driven to the ancient city of Kelsingra; their refuge and new beginning. 
 So this drives the novel forward, and gives the characters hope in an almost impossibly difficult situation. But, this is a Robin Hobb novel. So that means the story is paced out superbly with the journey only beginning as the book closes. She really knows how to add such depth to her world. From this point, I think this series has more potential than the LiveShip Traders. The story seems tighter and the characters more desperate. There's going to be some exciting times ahead reading the reading the next three books; it has been far too long Robin Hobb, the queen of fantasy.

I received a copy of this title to read and review for Wicked Reads 
 4 Stars. 
 I believe this goes without saying, this is not a standalone, as it's 14.5 in the Elemental Assassins series. Jennifer Estep has created a fascinating urban fantasy world- start at the beginning (Spider's Bite) with kick-butt Gin the assassin. 
 Unwanted is a short story narrated by Gin's brother, Finn, showcasing the aftermath of earlier events. Finn is suffering from guilt and a healthy dose of self-loathing after his mother tried to rob the bank where he is employed. After a few of his fellow employees were killed, his current coworker not only refuse to trust him, they blame him. But he blames himself too... 
 Attending a funeral, Finn overhears something he shouldn't featuring the widow of a fallen coworker negotiating with the local muscle over gambling debts amassed by her brother-in-law. To assuage his guilt, Finn becomes involved. 
 The first 15 - 20% of this short story had a lot of info dumpage, where Ms. Estep backtracks to play catch-up so the reader wouldn't be confused to the rest of the events of the story. I found myself skimming those portions, but read every word thereafter. If you aren't current in the series, please note this short story will be a spoiler then. 
 Many were undoubtedly upset with Finnegan after the last installment, and Unwanted gives his version of events, causing the reader to empathize while he tries to make amends.

My first Erica Spindler and it did not disappoint! It's everything you expect from a thriller - a sordid past, a murder mystery that brings the past the protagonist so desperately wants to leave behind, back to light, a twist or two and a conspiracy. What wouldn't you like about it? 
 Miranda Rader, or Randi as she was known as a child, didn't have the best childhood. One night, at the age of 15, leaves her feeling like she can't count on anyone. Sent to juvie, she vows to move forward, leave her past behind and go into law where she inevitably earns respect for her integrity. A murder of a prestigious professor who is a part of one of the richest and most respected families in town propels Miranda right back to her past when a newspaper clipping regarding that one fateful night is found at the scene. When a cop is found murdered shortly after, evidence starts pointing to Miranda as the killer. As truths come to light, she has to find a way around the law to prove her innocence as revelations start shattering her new found trust. 
 A very easy and fast read. Spindler draws you right into the story and the fast pace from the first chapter to the end puts this as a one-sit read. I found myself very involved with Miranda's character. I was mad when she was mad, frustrated when she was frustrated and over all just wanted things to go well for her for once. I think the twists were fairly easy to figure out but didn't think it took away from the pace of the story line. There were a couple of moments kind of thrown in that didn't quite make sense to me and if you've read this book, let's discuss! I won't go into here to spoil anything. Overall, a fantastic read and I'll definitely be looking forward to more of this author's work.

4.5 
 Much of what I said for the first book, 
 Slated 
 [review], still applies to 
 Fractured 
 - Kyla is still this intriguing little enigma of a person, and the book is still compulsively readable, with a very skin-crawlingly plausible (as an extreme) basis for a dystopia. As the series goes on and the reader is given more information and more of an insight into what's really happening, everything gets a little darker and more worrisome in a really interesting way. The more that is revealed, the more questions there are to ask. 
 I love the layers Teri Terry has presented in this story. There is intrigue, terrorism and patriotism, politics and science and double-crosses, all muddled up together into a full, tension-fraught, scarily real world. These elements play off of each other, each heightening the next and creating more tension and anticipation for what is to come - there are so many places things can start to go wrong, and the reasons things have come to this extreme are both horrifyingly believable and just-enough over the edge as to be almost too much. Kyla is an excellent representation of all of this; she is all these different people, stacked one in another like matryoshka. She's naive and innocent, but also strong, smart and uncanny. She's incredibly vulnerable and broken, but fierce and seemingly unbreakable. The things that have been done to her - and not just the Slating, but the layers and layers of things, which are hinted at in book 1 and explored more in book 2 - have created in Kyla quite an enigma, which doesn't quite fit anywhere, but has pieces of every aspect of this intricate world reflected in her. 
 The more Kyla understands about her world and herself, the more intriguing and dangerous everything becomes, and I love it! Of course, it helps that Terry's writing pulls you along at high speed. As with Slated, I Didn't intend to read this in a day, but I damn near did. Terry just makes it so easy to keep flipping pages; I had to know what Kyla was going to remember next, or how she was going to get out of every predicament. As the series progresses, new characters pop into Kyla's life with greater frequency, and who they are and their motivations are always suspect. With each new interaction, the stakes are raised, and you're left constantly wondering how things could possibly end well. And the beauty of the book? 
 Sometimes they don't. 
 That may sound strange to you, but think about what a beautiful thing that is, to not have everything clean and nice and tied up with a bow. Life isn't always clean and nice; life is hard. Sometimes things suck. Sometimes good people get hurt and bad ones keep on doing the hurting, and very little adds up or makes sense or feels right. That's life. In a dystopian society? It should be just that, but more. Things should be heightened, danger should be real, and it should feel as though maybe there just isn't a Happily Ever After. That's the only way I can really buy in, and I'm so glad that Teri Terry gets* that and doesn't cop out and wave a magic wand so that everyone comes out unscathed and perfect**, happy and whole. I appreciate that so much. 
 I appreciate the danger and the questions and the tension, and just GAH! is it time for book 3 yet?!
